ELECTION EXPENSES.

THE Labour Representation League re-
gusted an interview with Mr. GrAusToNE, for
the purpose prineipally, of urging on his atten-
tion the propriety of the Government adhering
to that portion of the Ballot Bill which
relieved candidates from the heavy expenses
usually denominated the legal expenses of
elections. Mr. GL.IDSTONE, as a matter of
Course, knows more about the matter than
anybody can tell him-. He is. thoroughly
acquainted with all that can be said in its
favour, or urged against it; and more than
this, he has found out, through the ministra-
tions of Mr. GLYNN', why this provision
should be carefully shut out from the Bill
brought in this Session. It was nothing but
natural, therefore, that to save time and
bother he should hand the Labour League
deputation over to Mr. FORSTER, 'and it was
just as natural that Mr. FORSTER, who, no
doubt, has as strong a disinclination to be
bored as his chief, should propose to " lump "
together two or three of these deputations,
that he might finish the whole thing with as
little palaver as need be, and without any
needless repetition of those stale Common-
places to which working men are usually
'treated when great men condescend to argue
with them on questions of political expedi-
ency.

Those deputations to members of the Ad-
ministration are usually very blundering
affairs. A dozen or twenty men, with the
average number of foOlish talkers amongst
them, are almost sure to Muddle anything
they take in hand to argue about. One or two
'may understand the ease thoroughly, and state
It well. And the Minister, if left in their hands
might be properly fastened down to the point or
points in which the strength of the ease lay ; but
at the critical moment some halt:informed idiotic
person is sure to strike in, and furnish the
loophole of eseape the puzzled official is
anxiously looking for. The web soon becomes
hopelessly entangled, and in the end the depu-
tation files off, and is bowed out with a sort of
inward consciousness of' having made a ridicu-
lous failure, except perhaps in the ease of the
gobbler, whose face is bright in the belief that
he had driven the right nail home and
clenched it in the most effeetual manner.
Two or three of these bodies would have
.furnished easy work to Mr. 'Fonsmt.. He
.would have knocked their heads together,
playing the nonsense of 'one off against the
'sense of another, and would have sent them all
'away much the Same as they had come, with
some din half-understood idea perhaps of the
advantage in argument one clever man has
over a crowd in whielt, though some few may
'be intelligent and ' able, others are so stupid
and garrulons, that the intelligence and ability
at hand cannot be turned to good account.

Mr, FousTEu knows this, and therefore,
naturally enough, wished all who meant to
come to make their appearance at the same
time. In refusing to be treated thus the
Council of the Labour Representation League
acted with good sense and discrimination as
well as with spirit. If the Council of this
body have given prtper attention to the
subject, for the promotion of which they have
organized their Association, they ought to have
certain positive and distinct ideas, which they
are capable of expressing, and should,
therefore, have an opportunity of uttering
these in their own way, and on their own
responsibility, without running the risk of
being confounded with persons with whose
opinions they might not agree, and for whose
action they could not in any way hold them-
selves accountable.
It is much better not to go on these deputa-
tions than not 'to be able to regulate the
conduct of those who attend, and so 'far as
this Ballot Bill is concerned, there is no use in
attempting to hold an interview with any one
of her MAJESTY'S Ministers, unless those who
engage in it have clear and distinct views to
express, and have at the same time a full and fair
opportunity of expressing them. Besides, the
real truth of the matter is the Government dare
not secede to the wishes of the working
men in this matter of Election expenses.
They don't want' working men in the House
of Commons. The presence of any number of
these, however small, would disturb that
balance of parties which is now so well
arranged, and so thoroughly understood by
party managers on both sides. An indepen-
dent few, capable of influencing the people
from the floor of the House of Commons, and
incapable of being managed by the opposing
"whips," would spoil many nice calculations,
• and render uncertain many of those plots and
plans by which political power is now so fre-
quently won and lost. •
Liberal members do not want working men
in the 'House, and they have removed all
.doubt on this head from the mind of the
PEMIE MINISTEn. Let any man in his
Senses ask himself what constituencies are most
likely to return 'working men, arid the answer
will 'be that only those now represented by
Liberals would even attempt to return them.
No, working Man would think of fighting North
Notts against the Dukes. To working man
would dream of contesting any division of the
Great York County. Land owners, rich
merchants, professional or learned bodies,
Would not vote for men whose only property
is their labour. Therefore, only in those seats
of industry where the working classes out-
number all other classes, can the working men
candidates have any chance whatever.
It we take any group therefore of such con-
stituencies in the manufacturing districts, we
shall find that as a rule they are represented by
persons belonging to the Liberal party. Can
,we therefore. be surprised that those persons
should oppose a provision in the Ballot Bill
which would bring into the field rivals
, to fight with theta for the possession of their
seats ? On this ground the Conservative's
would be much safer than the Liberals. Of
course their old prejudices will keep them
from
,voting for any measure which aims at
. liberalising or economising in conneetion with
our tleetiOns. Old-fashioned people 'do not
run after newfangled ways of doing things.
But if our Conservatives wore not so politically

duce them to make another flank movement,

doing so, is that they act- as an insurmount-
able barrier to the direct representation of
labour. They carry with 'ihem corruption,
and rut money power above Manhood. They
stamp a brand of inferiority on Man Of
humble position, Whatever their mental or
moral 'Owen They plitee on the worker a
mark whieh practically excludes 'him from the
full rights of citizenship, and which shuts
him out from the opportunity of legitimately
promoting the interests of labour in Parlia-
ment. And any man' who, through selfish
fears for his min position, aids in continuing
so odious and injurious an exclusion, should
have the active opposition of every honest
working man, whatever the other qualifica-
tions or recommendations of such a candidate
may be. LLOYD JONES.'

MEETING OF COMPOSITORS.

On Wedeesday night an aggregate meeting of
the compositors of London, society men, employed
on book and parliamentary work, was held at
Exeter-hall, to consider the reply from the master
printers to a memorial sent to them by the Trade
Committee, in pursuance of resolutions passed at a
delegate meeting hold a few weeks since, request-
ing a reduction in the working hours, and an ad-
vance in the rate of wages. .141 r. Lee occupied
the chair, end there were fully three thousand
men present.

The Chairman having briefly opened the pro-
ceedings, Mr. Self, the secretary of the trade
society, read a report, which stated that the
memorial sent into the master printers requested
that on and afor the Ist of March the working
hours should be 54 per week, or 9 per day, all
hours worked beyond that time to be paid for as
overtime, and each day to stand on its own merits,
and that an advance of id• per thousand upon all
work except newspaper work should take place at
the same time, the rate of wages given to estab-
lishment bands Paid by the week to remain as at
present. The result of this memorial was a con-
ference between the Trade Council and the Com-
mittee of ,Laster Printers, but the terms proposed
by the 'Committee were such as the Council were
unrible to accept. The Masters' Committee Posi-
tively refused to entertain the question of the
advance of a bal4enny per thousand letters in
any shape; and in place of 54 hours per week,
offered 57 hours, to be regulated in such way as
the. employers in each office might determine, and
that no overtime should be paid until 57 hours
had been actually worked
.in each week. The
Cominitten also made an alternative proposal togrant
the 51 hour, but clogged with such conditions as
would have made the coacession of no value. The
Council felt it their duty, in the interest of the
trade, to .reject the proposal of the Masters' Com-
mittee, and maintain tho terms of the memorial,
and had called the present meeting to take the
opinion of the whole of the trade upon the (pee-
tion.

A long and animated discussion ensued, the
result of which was the adoption of resolutions to
the following tired : —" That this sleeting adhere
to the terms of the memorial sent in by the
Council for the 51 hours per week, puro and
simple, with the advance of id. per thousand
letters upon all descriptions of work, except
newspaper and parliamentary work." " That
unless a favourable answer to the memorial be
received from the master printers .by Saturday,
the 16th instant, the men in every book Ace
shall give a fortnight's notice to the employer,
and that no overtime whatever be worked during
such fortnight.". These 'resolutions Were poised
almost unanimously with loud cheering, and a
vote of thanks *as given to the Council and the
Secretary for their conduct.

MINE4B' AGENTS.

Agreeably to an arrangement made at the con-
ference between the colliery owners and the
miner's delegates, hold on the 17th inst., an
adjourned meeting between the two bodies took
place on Saturday, at the Wood Memorial Hall,
Newcastle.
,There was a large attendance of the
masters,, Mr. Hugh Taylor, Chipchase, being in
the chair, Mr. W. Crawford, president of the
Durham Minors' Mutual Confident Association
acted as principal spokesman for the miners' dele-
gates, who were eight in number.
• At the last meeting the masters agreed to the
abolition of the yearly bond, and the first question,
therefore, taken into consideration at the present
conference, was the nature of the future agreement
between the masters and the men. On the one
hand, the employers suggested monthly notices on
both aides; but the men, on the other hand, were
unanimous in their request for a fortnightly
notice, with the option of either giving or receiv-
ing the same on any day except Sunday. After
some discussion, the masters acceded to the 'Wishes
of the men on this point.

The next question taken into consideration, was
the advance iii pay demanded by the Men. A
proposition for an increase of 35 per cent. on all
prices paid in April last, was submitted by the
delegates, who, in, answer to questions by the
owners, admitted, that the advance requested ap-
peared to be a large one, but they urged that it
Was Made in consequenci3 of the le* rate of re-
muneration received by the miners of the county
at the time referred to. To this advance the em-
ployers objected, on the ground that it was exces-
sive. They also urged that for several years past
coal had been low in the market, and the working
pits had been uniemunerative, and submitted that
it was unfair on the part of the workmen, when a
slightly better price had been obtained, to make an
exorbitant demand. They also pointed out that
the advance asked for was greatly in excess of that
obtained by the minor ii irkother parts of the coun-
try. To this argument the. delegates replied that
they were of opinion that the advance asked for
was not greater than the excessive profits of the
masters would allow thorn to pay in fact, they.
only wanted a reasonable ratio:of the profit made
by their labour, and they were also of opinion
that the 35 per cent. advance would not place the
miners of the county of Durham on an equality
with the workmen of other counties. After same
further disettssion, the delegates intimated that
they would be satisfied, if the owners did not feel
disposed to give the increase asked for, with the
' average score price paid in Northumberland and
South Yorkshire. They. wore willing, if the
a:raiders would divide the two last-mentioned
coUnties into four quarters each, and would seledt,
according to arrangement, two collieriea from each
of the eight quarters,-to accept the average of the
prices paid at the Sixteen collieries as the standard
scale in the county of Durham. The owners,
after hearing this propOsition, asked the deputation
if the average would be accrepte&by the men at
those collieries in the county who were at present
only working for 5 per cent. less than the proposed
standard. The delegates replied that every such
colliery would accept the average if the masters
would give it to the men of those collieries who
were at present working for 60 per cent. less than
the average named.

After some further dismission the delegates re-
tired. On being called back into the room they
were informed by the chairman that the owners
did not think it was desirable to go to either
Northumberland or South Yorkshire for an
average, as they were of opinion that they were
quite competent to manage their own affairs; and
that they had agreed, in a spirit of conciliation, to
offer an advance of 20 per cent, on all prices over
and shot% all censideration money paid in April
last. The 'deputatiott stated that they had no

authority to accept the offer of the owners, but
they would in due course communicate it to the
general body of the men. The conference then
broke up.

On Monday morning the operatives employea in

asters would not concede the nine hours system.
Por the last fortnight the operatives employed in

have been agitating for the nine hours. In an

lIADY asked for this without any reduction in
ages; and, with respect to those who were paid

enabled to earn the same amount of wages. These
demands were grounded on the argument that, as
'1
the adult males had obtained the nine hours

n 5,65 and Tennant, all of whom are large em-
ployers.

Master's and operatives, the former refusing to
concede the demand for the nine hours' limit, and

the latter being firm in their determination not to
return to their work unless the point is toneeded
to them..

At the Queen's Hotel, on Wednesday afternoon,
the masters held a meeting, and a resolution was
passed strongly supporting the employers in the
course they had taken with the workpeople who
are now out on strike.

A mass 'meeting of the operatives was held on
Wednesday evening, in the Assembly Rooms.

passed :-
1. That inasmuch as all able-bodied men
excepting those in factories have got the nine
hours, it is desirable that all the men, women, and

equal number of the masters at any time that will
suit their convenience to discuss the nine hours'
question fairly and honestly, and to see upon what

endeavour to fix upon a chairman as arbitrator

which we now enjoy.

articles.title: NORTH STAFFOR DS II RE. TUE MINERS.
articles.text:
NORTH STAFFOR DS II RE.
TUE MINERS.

A meeting of miners Wag held in the Town
Hall, Hanley, on Wednesday evening, to celebrate
the concessions which have lately been made to
the ruiners of North Stafford, in the reduction of
the working hours to 60 per week, and to hear an
address from Mr. Alfred A. Walton, upon the
benefits of union, and the necessity of still extend-
ing and strengthening their position in North
Stafford.

Mr. wmi&m Brown occupied the chair. Mr. Wal-
ton addressed the meeting for more than an hour,
pointing out the great advantages which the working
Men had obtained by union towards the close of the
last year and the beginning of the present; and
urged upon the working men of the district, both
miners and others, to beeomestill more firmly ouited,

not for the purpose of making any unjust demands
upon their employers, but for the purpose or main-
taining the advantages already obtained. If they
wanted to really understand the value of unions, and
what they had done for working men, they need only
contrast the condition of the agricultural labourers
in the rural district', where union was unknown,
and the rate of wages in all our largo towns and
centres of industry where the working men are
united. The poor unfortunate agricultural labourers
are getting only from nine and ten to twelve
shillings per week, while the mechanics and
artisans in town were getting from five to six shil-
lings a day.
Mr. Walton proceeded at considerable length
to contrast the positions of trades tuitions at the
present day compared to what they were from
thirty to forty years ago, and the great progress
that had been made in a better knowledge of the
true principles of combination. Mr. Walton also
pointed out the necessity for the direct repre3en•
tation of labour in Parliament, by returning
competent working men to the House of Commons
at the next election, and concluded an exhaustive
speech by urging upon the meeting the necessity
for carrying out the principles of trade unionism,
direct representation of hbour ,in Parlia-
merit, and also to turn their attention to the great
and important principles of co-operative produc-
tion. A resolution was also passed in favour of
international arbitration instead of war.

OLDHAM.

BRICKLAYERS TRADE AND BENEFIT SOCIETY.

The members of this branch of the organisation
held their annual meeting at the Bull's Head,
George-street, on Friday. The number of members
present on the occasion was above the average
usually attending the anniversary.
After the tiloth was withdrawn, a short business
meeting was held, at which the annual report was
read, which was as follows :
Ferzow Wonxturai,

The time has again arrived when we aro in duty
bound to take a retrospective glance at our posi-
tion, and I think we have reasons to be proud of
the success that has crowned our efforts. Although
the 11alanoe sheet does not show us to be in quite
so good a position financially as we were at the en 4
of 1870, still I think you will all agree that though
we were compelled to draw rather largely from our
funds in May, the money has not been misspent, and
that we are already receiving the benefit id the
outlay. •
am sorry to say that since our last report was
published one member and one member's wife have
gone to "that bourne from whence no traveller
returns," there has also been more than an average
number of accidents. "

On your last yearly day you decided that your
secretary should call a special meeting of the
Trades' Council, to consider the advisability of
sending a deputy to the Trades' Union Congteas,
to be held in London on the Bth of March last,
you offering to pay the expanse of calling the
meeting; consequently, through your instruments.
lity, the meeting was held, and a dt.puty ap-
pointed.

The year has been an eventful one—full ,of
interests of vital importance to the whole body. of
Trades .Unionists—serious obstacles have boon'
raiSed, and means devised, with the intent to cripple
the efforts as well as to weaken the energies of the
officers of oursocieties, so as to make their endea-
vours of non-effect.. No doubt most of you are,
quite aware that during the last Session of Parlia-
ment a Trades' Union Bill was introduced into at)
House, but some of its clauses were:so diametrically
opposed to the interests of trade societies that the
congress decided to object to them in every. pos-
sible and legitimate way; hence the deputation to
Mr. Bruce. The result was that the Bill was divided
into two separate parts, one-the Trades' Union Bill
proper, we will call it for distinction, a good and
useful Meiistne ; the other, call d the
," Criminal
Law Amendment Act," and a more obnoxious,
arbitrary, ambiguous, and one-sided piece of class
legislation it •is scarcely possible to conceive, a
standing diggrace to those who passed it into law,
and an unjust stigma upon every honest working
man in the country, presupposing, as it really
does (as far as
,Trades' Unionists are concerned)
criminal intentions in almost every Act they may
perform; it certainly repeals the old • combination
laws, but it enacts others far. worse.
It is also proposed to h&c° a PAH() Trades'
Demonstration, in Oldham, in April next, to pro-
test against it, after which a mass meeting will be
held, and some of the mcst noted Trades' Unionists
in the United Kingdom will be invited to speak.
After a short discussion it was adopted, and the
beat thanks of the meeting were awarded to the
secretary for preparing the same.
At the social meeting which followed, goodwill
and harmony was the order of the evening.

about 80 boiler makers ceased work.

abolition of frame rents and f tlarges ; and at a
recent Meeting of the local Board of Arbitration
the men consented to a deduction of 17* per. con,.

.terms of ;he "middlemen," who require them to

.winding, light, and heat. At a large Meeting of '
workmen, held in the Gladstone Hall on Tuesday
night, it was unanimously resolved that a weekly

in the week. It is reported that there is some

in-

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

Mr. Crawford, M.P., •presuled at a meeting,
held on Monday in Seething-lane, when reso-
lutions were passed expressing approval of the
Bill now before Parliament providing for the
abolition of compulsory metage dues in the
City, and recommending an impartial super-
vision in the discharge and weighing of all
grain arriving in the port of London.

An extraordinary meeting of the Birming-
ham Gas Company ma held on Monday, when
the committee of investigation presented a
report; showing that the defalcations of the
late seerstary, who absconded some months
ago, amount to about £40,000.

Two hundred and eighty patients were
relieved at the British Hospital for Diseases
of the Skin during the week ending March
2nd.

Sunday trading in the New-cut, Lambeth,
was the subject of another prosecution on
Monday at the Southwark Police-court, where
forty-six eestertnongers and tradesmen ap-
peared to answer summonses taken out by the
vestry. Very little testimony was, however,
adduced, and the magistrate adjourned the
further hearing until April 23, by which time
evidence will be forthcoming to show the re-
spective rights of the vestry and of private
individuals to the place where the alleged ob-
structions have been created.

A lodging-,house keeper, of Archibald-hill,
St. George's-in-the• East, was on Monday con-
victed at the Thames Police-court of having
kept a person upon his premises who was
suffering from small-pox,"withont notifying the
same at the nearest police station. A flee of
20s. was inflicted.

A large number of tradesmen in Exeter
have resolved to resist payment of the ineome-
tax. surcharges. The pods of an hotel-
keeper have already been distrained upon.

The Government of India has directed that
all naval and military officers, as well as civil
officials, aro to wear mourning for a month as
a mark of respect for the memory of the into
Viceroy. Public meetings or condolence have
taken place throughout India, whieh where
attended by all classes of Europeans and
natives, as well as by the Consuls of all
nations.

Writing upon the subject of the Alabama
question, a Correspondent in Washington
says that, while Americans almost universally
maintain that the Geneva Tribunal has a
right to decide as to the admissibility of the
claim for indirect damages, and that Great
Britain will be 'guilty of bad faith if she with-
draws from the arbitration, there is, neverthe-
less, a feeling of regret and surprise that the
question was not settled beyond all dispute
in. the Treaty itself. :And of the best American
authorities on international law, Professor
Woolsey, maintains that if the claims for
indirect damages were not to be submitted to
the arbitrators, it follows that they can at any
moment be revived, and thus become a fresh
(woe Of quarrel, Meanwhile the Correspon-
dent says the American public regard the
question with a calmness which is hardly dis-
tinguishable from indifference. It is oonsidered
that if England now withdraws from the
Treaty she will be the chief loser, and that the
responsibility will test with her. According
to an authority,eited by. the. Correspondent,
should the arbitrators, Instead of awarding
Ainerioa, a gross sum, refer the question of
damages to the Board of Assessors, the indirect
elaiMs will probably be dropped'.

The. number of passengers convoyed .over
I he. Metropolitan, Metropolitan and St. John's
IVond,, and ilammersinith and City Railways
on Tuesday, Veb. 27 (Thanksgiving Day), was
243,863 ; the number of passengers using the
Metropolitan Company's Omnibuses running
betweiqi Portland-road and ilegent-eiretts on
the balite day was 4,k523.

At the Birmingham relice-court onMonday,
John Elliot, wood turner, and Jane, his wife,
w-ore charged with eoining. About a fortnight
age a man was arrested in Coventry, and from
information he gave, the house of thci prisoner
was searched on Sunday, and about 200 base
florins, several moulds; and a galvanic battery
used in plating the coins, which were princi-
pally made of brass, were found. For some
time. past a quantity of base coin has been
circulated in the district, and there is no doubt
that it came from this person. Eliot was
committed to the Assizes, and his wife dis-
charged.

In further evldenco of wart of discipline in
the Andaman eunvict Set clement, we observe
a report in a Rangoon paper that three con-
victs recently escaped. from Port Blair. They
were acting, as watchmen of the schooner
Lady wrow, and in the night succeeded in,
securing the boat of the schooner, and mado
their escape without 'being detected. They
had not sines been heard of.

The Town Council of Stendal have unani-
mously resolved to present the freedom of the
town to Prince Bismarck. This is a strange
eiample of the irony, of history. Five hun-
dred years ago, the ancestors of Prince
Bismarck were forced to leave Stendal in
consequence of a rising of the lower classes,
at the instigation of the clergy, because thi3
head of the family had founded a school
which was not to be placed under the control
of the Chapter; and now the freedom of the
town is presented to the descendant in
acknowledgment of his efforts to liberate the
school from clerical influence.

On Monday morning, at Okel Tor; hear
Calstock, Cornwall, a woman named Nicholls
was horribly mutilated 1?y her husband who,
while she was soundly sleeping, out open her
abdomen in several places with a large clasp
knife. Her daughter and son-in-law, who
went to her assistance, was also injured by
Nicholls, who has been for some time past in a
very desponding state. The recovery of the
woman is believed to be impossible.

During the eleven months of the financial
year, ending on Saturday last, the Treasury
receipts amounted to £66,762,728, an inerease
of more than four millions and a quarter over
the sum in the corresponding period of last
year. The revenue from stamps already
exceeds the estimate by £1,88,000. The
expenditure has been £64,933,741. On tho
2nd instant the balance in the bank of England
was £7,536,662.

Clowns are popularly supposed to bear any
amount of punishment on the stage ; but
Joseph Elwell, the clown at Astley's,' haying
been struck with a carrot by a supernumerary,
retaliated with four !blows, fey which Mr.
Chance fined him £2 at:Lambeth Poliee-court.

An action to recover damages for breach of
promise of marriage was tried at the Hertford
Assizes on Tuesday, in which Miss Fanny
Key, the daughter of a manager to a brewery,
obtained £l,OOO from Mr. Powers, one of a
firm of millers at Biggleswade.

It is now announced front Versailles that
M. Pouyer-Quertier, the Finance Minister of
France, has definitively resigned his post, in
consequence of the objection taken by some
of his colleagues to his defenee of M. Janvier
do la Motto, the late Prefect of the Euro.

We learn from Berne that the revision of the
Swiss Constitution is now ended, and that the
National Colima and the Council of the States
have concluded their sittings.

Prinoe Frederick Charles of Prussia, who
has been paying a visit to Rome, has now left
that city for Naples on his way to Sicily.
During his stay in Rome all sorts of rumours
have prevailed as to the object of his journey.
The Clericals spread a report a little time
since that he was on IV mission in connection
with an alliance which would be highly fa-
vourable to their interests. It is now said
that the Prince has declared that in the event
of Italy being attacked by France she would
be defended by Germany.

News from the Cape of Good Elope by the
mail steamer which arrived at Southampton
on Tuesday states that Sir Henry 'Darkly has
been appointed Governor of West Griqualand,
which is the official name for the diamond
fields, Diamonds were still being sold by,
auction, but prices had declined. It is men-
tioned that spurious diamonds had been im-
ported into the colony from Birmingham.
From the gold fields favourable accounts
have been received.

Little hope exists—ticeerding to a report
addressed by the Duo de, Brcglia to the Foreign
Minister at Versailles—that any understand•
lug will be attained between the French and
English Goyerninents regarding the proposed
modifications on the Commercial Treaty. .

Before quitting office, M. Ponyer-Qnertier
performed .a stroke of business which recalls
the effective and arduous help he has renclered
to M. ThiorS in the'reatorative and liberative
efforts of the past twelvemonth; he signed
drafts for 330 millions of francs, in payment
of what remains due of the fourth half-
milliard of the war indemnity.

A meeting of the subscribers to the Fleet-
street Decoration Fund, 'convened by circular,
was held on Monday evening, when the fol-
lowing resolutions were passed unanimously:
--" That the sum of £2O from the surplus
fund and the ecarlet cloth on hand be presented
to Kin's College Hospital; that £2O be pre-
sented to the Farringdon doneral Dispensary;
and 1.10 to the Police Orphanage, as an
acknowledgement of the efficient services of
the police on Thanksgiving Day." A cordial
vote of thanks to Messrs. Bonnewell and Brad-
ford closed the proceedings. The presentation
Bibie was on view, and wa.sgreatly admired by
the subscribers and a number of their lady
friends who came to see it. It was forwarded
to General ICnollys at Marlborough-house on
Tuesday.

By the sudden death of the Earl of Lons
i -
dale, n his 85th year, Mr. Henry Lowther,.
the late Earl's nephew, who has sat for West
CuMberland since 1847, will be called to the
House of Lords. The deceased peer, who
was never married, was first returned to the
unreformed Parliament as far back as 1808,
and successively represented Cookonnouth,
Dunwich, and Westtnoreland, in the .House
of Commons. The new Earl's appointment
by Mr. Disraeli to the Lord-LieUtenaney of
Cumberland' and Westmoreland gave rise to
an interesting debate in the Uouse of Coin-
mons early in the session of 1869.

The nomination for Wallingford will take
place to-day (Saturday).

At a meeting of the Court of Aldermen on
Tuesday a letter was read from the HOMO
Secretary, conveying her Majesty's entire ap-
probation of the exCellent arrangements which
were made by the City Authorities for the
preservation of order on the 27th ult.

Tho inhabitants of Lambeth who have op-
pose(' the scheme of the Government for
building a convict prison upon Denmark-hill
will be glad to learn that the design has now
been abandoned.

On Tuesday the Committee of the Congre-
gational Union of England and Wales unani-
mously adopted a resolution, approving of
some of the features in the Scotch Education
Bill, but objecting to those provisions of the
measure which violate the principles of rah-
gious equality.

The Bishop of L'ival, after a canonical
inquiry, has authorised and required belief in
new miracle. He certifies that on January
18, 1871, the Virgin Mary appeared in person
to four children in the hamlet of Portmain.
The Bishop, moreover, undertakes to say that
the Supernatural fact was a genuine one, and
the devil had nothing to do With it. In conse-
quence, ho calls upon the faithful to subscribe
and build a church, to be called "-Notre Dame
de Portmain," on the spot where the four in-
fants saw the apparition. .

A mysterious paragraph about a police
search in the house of an old Bonapartist is
explained to relate• to M. Vitu, at one time
editor of the Oonstitutionner It is true that
his papers were overhauled on Tuesday, and
that Ile was under arrest for two or three
hours, but he is now at large.

Primary education in Switzerland is to be
under the supervision of the Confederation,
instead of being, as hitherto, left to the care of
the several Cantons. The resolution effecting
this change, which will have a serious bearing
on the religious or denominational question in
edueation, passed the Council of States by the
tiarrOw majority of 19 to 18.

The first jury ce.so in the Bankruptcy
Court occurred on 'Monday. 'Under the new
Aot, a jury may be empannellecl to try issues
of fact which cannot be settled by affidavit.
This trial was to ascertain the right of the
trustee of one Rawlings, a bankrupt, to a
traction engine which had been manufactured
by him and sent out on trial.

A serious charge of embezzlement was heard
at Southwark, on Monday. John Dunlop,
clerk to Mr. Henley, wine and spirit merchant,
Tooley-street, having appropriated about
XlOO, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to
six months' hard. labour.

Berjeant Ballantine on Tuesday asked Lord
Penzance to suggest some method by which
Sir Charles Mordatint might obtain a decision
in the suit against his wife, so that he might
either appeal to th 3 House of Lords, or go on
with the case. Alter a short discussion it was
agreed that the matter should stand over for a
week.

Last week tho aggregate mortality in
London and twenty other large towns of the
United kingdom was at the rateibf twenty-
six deaths annually to every 1,000 persons
estimated to be living. In the metropolis,
2,051 births and 1,423 deaths were registered,
the former having been 380, and the latter
212, below the average. Thirty-two persons
died from small-pox, 41 from measles, 21
from scarlet fever, 5 from diphtheria, 95
from whooping-cough, 21 from different forms
of fever (of which 3 were certified as typos, 12
as enteric or typhoid, and 6 as simple continued
fever), and 10 from diarrbon. The tempera-
ture was slightly •below the average on Tues-
day and Wednesday last, while a largo excess
prevailed on each of the other days, and the
mean of the week was 45.6 deg. and 5.6 deg.
above the average for the corresponding week
in 50 years. On Friday and Saturday the
temperature was equal to that of average days
in the middle of May.

Training stations for the several artillery
districts in England are at onoe to be estab-
lished, in accordance With one of the provisions
of Mr. Cardwell's ohm.° for the reorganization
of the army.

The Queen, who had contemplated institu-
ting a medal as a reward for long or faithful
service among her Majesty's domestic servants,
has inaugurated the institution by conferring
on Mr. John Brown, her personal attendant,
a medal in gold, with an annuity of
£25 attached to it, as a mark of her appre-
ciation of his presence of mind and of his devo-
tion on the occasion of the attack made upon
her Majesty in Buckingham Palace Gardens
on the 29th ult.

Charged with obtaining money under false
pretences, Mr. Frederick Cox, described as
honorary secretary Of the Free Dormitory
AsSoeiation, appeared beta.° Mr. Newton,
the Marlborough-street Police-00ml. It w:t4
alleged that by means of -illegally using; the ,
names of several well-known noblemen aad
ministers of religion, he had succeeded in'
collecting £3,0,00 last year, besides two sums
of £l,OOO each, sent by anonymons clew"'
the whole of which money he had fraudulently
used for his own purposes. Eventually the
case was adjourned for a few days, the defen-
dant meanwhile being liberated on his own re'
cognisauces.

IVilliam Holey, convicted, of having ,robbed
his employer and eloped with his wile, was
sentenced by Sir William Bodkin . at tile
Middlesex Sessions on Tuesday, to tWelve
months' imprisonment with hard labour, while
the woman, who charged her husband with
cruelty and threatening to kill her, was at the
request of the jury, taken into custody on the
charge of perjury.

Two youthful housebreaker, aged 12 and
10, wore convieted of having entered a hons°
at Wandsworth by removing a pane dgl
and stealing, amongst other things, some ow
coins and a knife. Each prisoner had iwn
convicted before, and their mailer pve the
elder one a bad charaCter. Mr. Bridge nom'
mitted the younger for four days, With ten ,
strokes from a birch-rod, the elder boy being .
remanded to be sent to a reformatory. ass,

The Speaker's lev6es are postponed till after
Piaster, in consequent* of the death of Mrs.
Vernon, the right hon. gentleman's sister.

At the Middlesex Sessions, William Jan.,. a
young printer, was found guilty of stearimg
plate from his master, Mr. Burrell. Mias
Woods, the master's niece, had assisted him,
under intimidation, as she urged; but the
Assistant Judge thought there had been
familiarity for the purpose of robbery between
them, and sentenced the man to twelve month.;
hard labour.

An open verdict was returned by the
coroner's jury in the case of the woman Duck-
worth, who arrived at her home in Somers
Town with a wound in the abdomen from
which she died. Her husband had bean
drinking with her, and was taken up by the
police; after which she drank with a cobbler.
Her own account btated that the wound was
self-inflicted; but this does not seem probable,
nor was any weapon found by which it could
have been caused.

A petition was lodged on Monday after-
noon last, in the Election Petition Office,
Dublin, against the return of Mr. It. P. Bien-
nerhassett as the representative of the county
of Kerry in the Imperial Parliament.

During a discussion in the Belgian Chamber
on the desirability of retaining a Minister at
the Papal Court, the belief was declared, nn
behalf of the Government, that the Minister
should be retained, "to defend the moral and
religious interests of the majority of the Bel-
gian population."

•
"Not Guilty," on all counts of the hichct-
ment, was the verdict found on Monday by
the jury before which M. Janvier de in Motto,
Prefect of the Eure, was tried on the charge
of malversation of. public funds. The pm:
ceedings' which have lasted a week, have excite('
great interest both in and beyond France'
and the triumphant character of the defence,
to which men of the highest credit and poi-
tion contributed—among them the Finn CO
Minister himself—has been not the least sin-
gular feature in the case, betraying as it dia
the irregularity of the principles on which
French official finance is knowingly con-
ducted,
.‘

M. Pouyer-Quertier's evidence in favotir of
M. Janvicr de In llotte has cost him his pitt,e!
as Minister. of Finance. In court, he el'
strongly against the conduct of M. DOW',
the Minister of 'Justice, in prosecuting a SU"
claim for a sum of £8,500 without the know'
ledge and counter-signature of the rina9°
Ministf-x—affirming that M. de la Motto reav,"
Y
did not owe the money. M. Dufaure Iv"
backed by one or two other ministers, Iv"
made M. Pouyer-Quertier's retirement a-0011:
'claim of their remaining. It is believed tho
M. Casimir-Perier, who quitted the Ministry
of tho Interior some, weeks ago in umbrage at
the Protectionist vote on the Treaty of Com-
ineree, will return to office with the portfolio
of Finance.

The circumstantial assertions that the Pope
had decided to quit Rome are contradicted by
the correspondent of the Daily Telegraph,
Who was admitted. on Friday to an audience,
and telegraphs that he was personally assured
by the Holy Father that he has no intention
of leaving Rome, " unless circumstances at
present unforeseen should compel him to take
that step." The despatch adds :—" The
health of Pius IX. is now wonderfully good,
and he seems to be most hearty and cheerful."

The Times correspondent at Rome, while
disbelieving that the Pope intends again to
convoke the (Ecumenical Council, or that he is
preparing to leave Rome, speaks of a party
desirous of his departure, who continue to
toil and agitate to that end, and says prepara-
tions are made which would render the carry-
ing out of the resolution easy and rapid were
it once taken.

The German officers in the Russian army
have published an appeal to all subjects of the
German Empire resident in Russia to celebrate
the birthday of the Emperor William, which
occurs on the 22nd of March. It is intended
to give a public banquet, and the question of
organising a national fete is Under considera-
tion.

A Vienna paper publishes the following from
Constantinople:—" The Porte having addressed
a friendly inquiry to the Russian Government
relative to the arming of the Black Sea fleet,
Prince GortsChakoir replied that the arming of
twenty-five vessels has taken place with the
sole end of experimenting on their manceu-
vering capabilities and exercising their crews.
The reply adds that the Government does not
intend to construct any more large vesSels in
the Ports of the Black Sea, or to augment the
numbers at present in those waters.'

The Times Prussian correspondent describes
Westerwell, who has now been handed over
to the criminal court on the charge of con-
spiring against the life of Prince Bismarck,
as a young man of twenty-six, who is said to
be spending the greater part of his day in
Prayer. "Like Pie None," the correspondent
adds, "he attaches considerable importance to
the intercession of the Holy Virgin, to whose
service he has devoted life and thought."
His parents are Count Vilain and Countess
Chlapovska.

The Times correspondent at Berlin tele-
graphs that the German ambassador at Paris
has been ordered home to report upon the
stability of the French Government, and
that military measures have been taken to
Provide for all contingencies in the occupied
departments. The same writer says it is
thought that the San Juan case will probably
go against' England. He adds the statement
that all the non... German Jesuits and monks
have been ordered to leave the Polish districts
of Upper Silesia.

A. credit of half a million florins, Emended
of the Reichsrath of Austria, by Govern-
ment, is intended for the temporary assistance
of necessitous Roman Catholic) Priests,, until
their income shall, be regulated by the new
law,, which is being prepared on the subject,
and which is already in a forward state.

A decree of the Minister of Public Worship
in Austria orders that none of the documents
issued by the Old Catholic parties, or the
action of their priests shall be recognised by
the State.

The Independance Beige publishes a des-
Patch from Berlin, according to which, at a
preliminary meeting of Liberal members of the
„Upper House, 40 votes were ascertained to be
lovourable to the Government Schools' Inspec-
tion Bill. Numerous approvals having, more-
over, beenreceived from the provinces, the bill,
It was thought,would wou pass.

A Ministerial circular has been published
which orders the reservation of a portion of all
cemeteries for the interment of non.Catholios
in Spain.

A.n incident of some note hits ocevred in the
debate at Versailles on the law against the
International Society, It was opposed by an
Internationalist Deputy—M. Tolain, of
Geneva Conference and Crenzot strike no-
toriety. He compelled the Right to listen to
a lengthy exposition a the real aims and
operations of the society, which were repre-
sented to have none of the wickedness
ascribed to them, but a great deal of good
with svhieh they have not been credited.

Speaking to an English deputation, M.
Tillers has promised that the revived pass-
port system in France, necessary now to
baffle Communist refugees and Bonapartist
Agents, shall cease as soon as possible. The
' President declared himself in favour of a
through service al Mont Cenis ; and of the
Practicability of a tunnel below the Channel
+—to which France could not give capital,
though 01,917 encouragement and facility
Would be given to its promoters.

Another deputation waited upon the Chan-
cella of the Exchequer' on -Wednesday, some
of whom urged the abolition of Schedule D of
the income tax, while others argued in favour
of all incomes under £2OO beinc, exempted
from the impost. Mr. Lowe pointed out the
impossibility of complying with the wishes of
his hearers with respect to the suppression of
Schedule D, and in reminding them that the
tax was raised last year solely in consequence
of the action of the House of Commons,
intimated that the best thing to be done was to
perfect the machinery by which the impost was
raised.

A largely-attended meeting was hold on
Wednesday evening at the Cannon-street
Hotel, when the Butchers' Trade Society
discussed at some length the steps necessary
to prevent the abolition of slaughter-houses
in the metropolis.

Last week the total number of paupers in the
metropolis was 122,045, of whom 35,330 were in
workhouses and 86,715 received out-door relief.
Compared with the years 1871, 1870, and 1869,
these numbers showed a decrease of 31,584,
58,956, and 28,774 respectively. The number
of vagrants relieved was 843,

The medical attendants on the Prince of
'Wales have recommended his Royal Highness
tcr pass the spring in the South of Europe.
Although the Prince's recovery is thus far
most satisfactory, it is desirable that the
strength should be entirely recruited before
his Royal Highness engages in public affairs.

The Rev. W. S. Helps, recently inhibited
by the Bishop of Rochester from officiating in
his diocese, has given in his adhesion to the
Liberation Society.

The death is announced of Mr. Angus
M'Pherson, secretary of the Highland Society,
and translator of the Queen's Diary in tlw
Highlands into Gaelic.

M. Spencer Ponsonby, Comptroller of the
Lord Chamberlain's department, is gazettod a
C.B. It is, also announced that Lord Polti-
more has been appointed Treasurer of her
Majesty's Household, in the room of Lord de
Tabby, resigned, and that Sir Hercules Robin-
son, late Governor of Ceylon, is to be Governor
of New South Wales.

On Wednesday Vice-Chancellor Bacon gave
judgment in the suit brought by the Union
Bank of London against Lord Ebury, the Chair-
man, four otherdirectors, and the Secretary of
the Watford and ,Rickinausworth Railway
Company. The object of the suit was to have
the directors of the railway company declared
personally liable for the payment of over
£20,000, due to the bank. The directors,
having been pressed for the payment of their
debt, deposited with the bank certain share
certificates and mortgage deeds, which turned
out to be worthless. The question was,
whether, by acting as they did in. making
representations on the faith of which the
bank were induced to accept as collateral
security for the debt due to them, docu-
ments which were of no more value than the
paper upon which they wore written, Lord
Ebury and his co-directors had incurred per-
sonal liability to make good such representa-
tions. His Honour deeided in the affirmative,
and that the directors must pay to the bank
.the whole amount remaining due.

The suit of Partington v. Partington and
Townend, whioh occupied the Divorce Court
four days, and wherein the petitioner was a
clergyman, has terminated in the dismissal
of the petition, with costs.

At the Guildhall Police Court, on Wednes-
day, a carman, was fined in a small penalty
for having wilfully damaged some hoarding
on the Thames Embankment belonging to the
Metropolitan Board of Works.

At the Worship-street Police Court, Amelia
Hemswith, lately brought up for theft, and
whose case has created some attention from the
peculiar circumstances under which tho aeon -
sation was brought, was discharged with a
caution on Wednesday.

The two policemen, Cook and Ewins, who
were lately committed to the Middlesex
Sessions on a charge of burglary, on Wednes-
day appeared to answer the indictment, but
no evidence was offered for the prosecution,
and a verdict of acquittal was consequently
returned.

Edward Dainty, an inmate of the Surrey
County Lunatie Asylum, was on Wednesday
committed for trial from tile Wandsworth
Police Court, charged with the wilful murder
of another inmate, named Mountain,
In The ease of the explosion which took place
at Mr. henry Gladstone's Cartridge Works,
at Greenwich, on January 18th, and whieh
resulted in the death of George Alfred Sargent,
the jury on Wednesday returned an open
verdict.

Mr. F. B. Marriott, the local coroner, opened
an inquest on Monday, at Lowestoft, on the
body of the poor woman Warnes, who was
murdered by her husband on Sunday while he
was suffering from delirium, induced by small-
pox. The jury viewed the body of the deceased
through a window of the cottage in which she
lived. As the unhappy man Warnes is still
in a state which precluded his presence at the
inquest, the coroner adjourned the inquiry for
three weeks.

At a special meeting of the Board of Works
on Monday, it was decided not to entertain
the proposal of the Crown to sell to the Board
that -portkon of reclaimed land on the Victoria
Embankment now used as a public) garden,
and leased at a rental by the Board. The
amount of purchase money was proposed to
be.settled by arbitration, but this project the
Board declined, while expressing willingness
to negotiate on the basis of the report made
by a select committee of the House of Corn-
'nuns.

The hundred and third day of the Ticb.
borne trial witnesssed the complete collapseoff
that extraordinary case, amid every sign o
popular excitement. When the court opened
Serjeant Banautili° spoke of the deolamtion
made by the jury on Monday as one which
was not quite clear to his mind. Did the jury
mean to convey that they had satisfied them-
selves solely upon that portion of the case
which was known as the tattoo marks, or had
they formed their opinion in relation to the
evidence set forth in the entire case? The
jury retired for half an hour, and on their
return the foreman stated that their decision
was based upon the entire evidence, as well
as upon that which related to the tattooing.
Serjeant nallantine then elected to be non,
suited. The judge expressed his concurrence
in the finding of the jury, and believing that
the claimant had been guilty of wilful and
corrupt perjury, directed him to be prosecuted
at the Central Criminal Court. His Lordship
fixed the bail at £5,000 in the plaintiff's
own recognisauces, and two sureties of
£2,500 each, or four of £1,250 each. The
Attorney-General undertook that ths prosecu-
tion should be at the public expense: A
warrant for the claimant's apprehension
was at once issued, and he was lodged in
Newgate in the course of the afternoon. The
Chief Justice, before closing the court, took
occasion amid .loud applause, to express his
entire belief in the evidence of Mrs. Rad-
cliffe.

A list of the dotations recently granted to
the German generals and statesmen by the
Emperor William has now been published.
Prince Frederick Charles Count Moltke and
Generals you noon and Charles,
have each
received 300,000 thalers each. Five others
have' received 200,000 thalers. Twelve
have received 100,000 thalers. A large
sum has also been placed at the disposal of
the King of Bavaria for distribution to his
generals.

The Post eorretipondent remarks that Pius
IX. is really worried among the conflicting
ambitions which surround him ; but it is not
to be 'supposed that he-Will leave ItOm merely
in obedience to the intimations of the
Jesuits.

It has already been announced that the
Austrian Government has refused the "Old
Catholics" as a. religious body, or to regard
the acts of their priests as valid. The reason.
for this is given in the circular issued by the
Minister of Public Worship. Re says that
the "Old Catholics" must be considered as
belonging to the Catholic Church: until they
form themselves into a distinct religious cont.
.rmunity. When they do so, and make a formal
declaration to the authorities to that effect,
they will enjoy all the advantages secured to
other sects by the. constitution. Until then
they will have no legnl existence which the-
Government can recognise, and consequently
all marriages contracted before "Old "
priests are declared null and void.

The working flax-spinners of Leeds are at
variance with their masters -on the hours of
labour. The former want the working day
reduced to nine hours; the latter, rather
than yield, threaten to remove their machinery
to Ireland, where, they ohuokling say, labour
is cheaper. We shall see. If, by methods
such as this, English operatives be thrown
upon the parish, Government will be obliged
to take up the emigration question with
seriousness.

The Limmer Asphalte Company, which has
the contract to pave Cornhill, was to have
commenced operations there on the Ist instant.
The Commissioners of Sewers, however, have
resolved that the footways in that thorough-
fare as well as the roadway shall be paved
with asphalt°. But before the footways are
so paved a new line of granite kerbstone has
to Wald, and the Limmer Asphalt° Company
await the completion of that part of the
undertaking before they commence operations.

articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOR P.ROMOTING TRE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO TILE IVOItIgNG CL &WM OF GRBAT 1111ITAIN.

FELLOW. Wonioinisr,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
us consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Chureh and State must be yeferred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation, of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legisl•tture to
apply the principle of that measure to ti e rest of
the United Kingdom. He was met with the objec-
tion that the case of lrelind was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland; did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to B}lofr that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
,Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Miall, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This 'unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted; and the Society for the Liberation
of _Religion from State-Patronage and Control ha
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after the broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
-a declaration of their hottest and deliberate" senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall; and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
loader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and alio as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working , Men, therefore, to answer that appal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among
,the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in 'favour' of, or against; the Dis-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland;- but also,
and perhaps • especially, with.. a view- to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General -Election, 'whensoever that. may, take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tnted, does not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
withdut taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
each Member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's C.ouniiitteo for promoting the
Separation of Churchand State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Conimittee may be thus con-
steely stated-
1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker. •

2. They nro of opinion that, since the • State
Church in one part of the, United Kingdom has
been disestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent ,not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
ingdpni
3. They are persuaded from obiervation and
experieuco,l that the State-Church has' utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established"; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk or the
Irish ,People were Roman
.Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish
ment.

6. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though the common • propeity
of the whole nation, are distiibuted among the
religious teachers of halt; or. less than half, of the!
people. Enormous and, disproportionate salaries
and emoluments are paid to Bishop) and other
Dignitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the. parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the foi rat
parishioner's, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations.
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment ía
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. hence, in every agitation ot a
political or social.,eharacter, they are always on
one side and the People on the other..
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides the nation into two
hostile partial. It prevents good men uniting, as
they otlier*ise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in
.movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life., ,

,
Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their follow workmen throughout the country.

In order, to ascertain and give effect to their views, .
