SATURDAY, MARCH 9, 1872.

THE LIBERAL PARTY SPLIT.
Mn. DrxoN's Education resolutions have
been negatived, and Mr. Foust' En's amend-
meat has been carried; but neither the de-
feat of the former nor the triumph of the
latter, can be considered as either great or
decisive. The 335 who voted against the re-
solutions, and the 323 who supported the
amendment, comprised all the Conservatives
in the House, while the minorities (91 and
98) consisted of advanced Liberals and Non-
conformists, every one of whose votes has
been needed by Government already, and will
be wanted more than ever, ere the session
closes.

The points embraced by Mr. DIXON'S motion,
were, the comparative failure of the Act in prac-
tice, the non.compulsion of attendance, partial-
ity and irregularity as to remission in payment
of school-fees; but chiefly the last, as show-
ing, that the Act allows Boards to pay fees ,
out of rates levied upon the' community to
denominational schools over which the rate-
payers have no control; that it permits Boards
to use the ratepayers' money for religious
instruction in schools; that it thus provokes
religious discord, and violates the rights of
conscience. In his- speech, the mover dwelt
forcibly on the notorious deficiencies Of most
of the schools thus favoured, and he
.de-
mended, in the name of a large and growing
section of the community, a complete separa-
tion of secular from religious instruction. _

To Mr. Rica Ann, followed by Mr. Lima(AS
and Mr. AUBEILON HELLBENT, it was reserved
to state and enforce the objections on the
ground df fairness as between. different
religions. The members sitting in Opposition,
said the member for Merthyr, wore the Ph
for which Mr. FOOTER angled, and he caught
them as fast' as he could throw his line. For
the Dissenters, all their efforts to preserve
harmony on the Liberal side had been either
rejected or defeated by the Government.
By the Government in combination with their
Whig friends and their opponents genorallft
but, on one occasion, by the manceavres
Ministers, even when all the independent men
of their own party were ashamed to felle/
them. He again warned the PRIME
that the Act as it now stands, is not satisfac-
tory to any one representative body of Pr°-
testant Nonconformists. There was something
very significant in the manner, as well as in •
the substance, of one of Mr. RICIINILD7
reminiscences of a former session. The
Member for Bradford (meaning, not Mr'
FORSTEIIO but Mr. MULL), repeated the pro;
test on the very night the Bill was goilig Utt

of Committee, and so excited the ire of the
PRIME MINISTER, that the right honourable
gentleman came as near swearing as a man Of
hishigh character could.
As to the conscience Clause, and the anti-
catechism clause, both are illusory. The
one is a mockery in the case of dependent
parents, and the other useless, because any
amount or kind of religious teaching can be
given without producing a written or printed
formulary, In short, the Bill became an Act
for the consolidation and perpetuation of sec-
tarian edtioation. Out or :-1,327 applications
for huildin; aml enlarging grants, more than
tw..)-thirds have been 2.111/10VeLl, Ulla nearly
all denominational, that is, Church schools.
And now, besides all this, they are to be sub-
sidised out of the rates. In these sChools,
thus to be sustained at the cost of
,all sects,
the pupils are, in &any instances, taught to
look upon all Dissenters as heretics, guilty of
heinous sin, and to be excommunicated with
bell, book, and candle, if, as one of the books
used puts it, "the law of the land did not
forbid the wholesome law of the Church to be
acted upon."
Although. Mr. LETnAM took the same side
as Mr. DixoN, he regretted that the battle-
field had n'ot been narrowed. For example, he
did not believe that education by direct com-
pulsion, unless restricted to the etiminal
and pauper classes, who have forfeited for the
time their independeace, was in accordance
with the feelings, habits, and opinions of the
people. A More. urgent question was raised by
the attempt to enforce the 25th
,clause, which
even the VICE-PRESIDENT only defended in a
,balf.hearted manner. Nothing could exceed
the anger and bitterness that clause had
given rise to on every side. He could see no
distinction between the maintenance of a
school and the maintenance of the. school
Systems or doctrines it was founded or Carried
on to promote. At the National Society's
Schools the whole school-time of the child was
a gradual leading of him up to communion
With and absorption by the Church. To such
schools Dissenters. are asked to contribute—
sehoo6built not to editcate, but to indoctrinate
the people. In sonic schools the amount
raised by school fees is so large, that, when
added to the denominational grant, the
managers are absolutely obliged to reduce the
voluntary aubioriptions for fear they should
have a surplus, and so be compelled to forfeit
a portion of the grant. In other oases, the
school fees, together with the denominational
grant, sulfide to discharge the whole expenses.
We are, therefore, rapidly coming to this—that
denominational schools not only receive a
grant in consideration of their secular teaching,
but will soon teach their sectarianism wholly,
or almost wholly, at the expense of the State,
Mr. LEATIESU put the operation of the Con-
science Clause in a lively light. The cate-
chism used , in a certain, school asked the
question, "In what light must we ,view those
who ,have never, been baptised ? " The pupils
are taught to answer, " A s heathens, whether old
or young:' At the ringing of a bell, the
Dissenters' ohildren are sent home, and then
the teacher proceeds to instruct those who
remain to regard those who are gone as
"heathens." And in doing this, the managers
are to be paid out of rates to which the " hea-
then " are contributors, equally with these
precious 'Christians themselves!
Of all men in the world, Dr. Ixori PLAN-
'AiIt• rushed to the , rescue. The measure he
affirmed, 'had succeeded marvellously. It
was 'the duty ef the Department, he argued,
to promote secular education, and no part of
its duty to prevent •-
religious instruction, Yet
that was the point to which the controversy
was now, coming. It was
as 1. 1 a person
wanting to buy Tizzl-Nyso,,s Poems should. try
to make it•a condition with the bookseller that
he should not at the same time sell a Bible to
another person: If he wanted to feed a sheep
for the dinner table, he could not prevent
part of the grass going to the formation of
Wool, though that Was no part of his primary
objea if the ratepayer went in ioco parentis,
te" pay the _fees for an indigent child, he. paid
for religious as Well as secular. instruction;
but he paid very little. The 25th clause he
.
admitted, WAS exceedingly dangerous in its
°Urdu', as well as in its refusal because,

unless exercised with great prudence, it would
produce an educational pauperism throughout
the country. The Act was stigmatised as con-
current endowment, which was a bad term; and
in the eyes of Dissenters acted like a red flag to
a bull. If it had not produced so much noise
and dissatisfaction, he should have thought
the liberty given to the parent either to refuse
religion altogether, or to select that which
suited himself and his child, would have been
ample compensation for the slight pressure put
upon the ratepayer. The ratepayer's conscience
was difficult to understand. It was vague and.
general, and only quickened into activity by
politioll agitation; but the parent's conscience
was personal and individual, and easily acted
upon by a sense of parental responsibility.
Therefore, when they gave the parent liberty
of conscience, the ratepayer's conscience might
very well have been kept out of sight. It was
impossible to carry out compulsory education
unless accompanied by a denominational
system. Not a single magistrate in the king-
dom would fine a parent or send him to prison
for refusing to send his children to school if he
pleaded that the school had no religion, or a
colourless religion; but it was a different
thing if the magistrate could refer to a school
of the parent's own persuasion.
This sounds plausible enough; but it will
not bear the test of practical experience,
which gives parents the mere mockery of rights
of conscience in the matter. As Mr. AUBERON
HERBERT clearly showed, the Act pretended
one thing, and its framer took care that it
should really do quite another thing. An
instance in point occurred near Notting-
ham. The School Board was elected on the
20th of April, and on the 19th of June asked
permission to build a school for 010 children.
They tried to raise the money from the Loan
Commissioners, but could not without consent
of the Privy Council. Having obtained that
consent in November, in December they re-
ceived a.letter from the department, not quar-
relling with the estimate, but suggesting that
there should be a separation between the boys,
girls, and infants, that the denominational
accommodation should be increased for the
boys, and that the girls and infants should .be
left to them. Now, if it were the duty of the
State to give religious teaching, where was it
to stop? If a person were too poor to pay for
his children, and he were, say a Jew or a
Roman Catholic, it would be equally the duty
of the State to build a synagogue or a Roman
Catholic school for him. Surely it would be
far better for so rich a body as the National
Society eto pay the school fees of children
whose parents were too poor to give them
religious teaching, than to call on the State
to give them
.religious instruction. He ad-
vocated tolerance to all, even to those who,
in this age of free thought, were not attached
to any Church at all. While secular educa-
tion was of general interest, religious teach-
ing was a class interest, because every one
who attempted to define it would define it
according to his own particular views. We
must deal out justice fairly and equallj, to all,
and justice can only be done in this case
by establishing a purely secular' system of
education.

The appeal of Mr. HERBERT to the National
Society, reminds us of the wise as well as
liberal course which we understand the next
most powerful " denomination," the Wesleyan
Methodists, to have resolved upon taking;
namely, to pay out of their own pockets, the
fees of all those children in their schools whose
parents are unable; a course which they are
taking to preserve the high charaoter of those
schools, and prevent them from the degrading
and pauperising influence of suoh payments
out of rates as the twenty-fifth section of the
Act sanctions.

In the meantime, Mr. FORSTER, appears to
have been requested by his chief to give way
before the rising and swelling storm. Having
defended himself with vigour, if not with com-
plete success, he offered a compromise to the
objeotars. Mr. MUNDELLA. had given notice
that, in
the event of Mr. FORSTER'S amend-
ment to Mr. DixoN's motion becoming the
main question, he would move a resolution to
the effect, " That it is desirable that the
Education Act of 1870 should be amended so
as to secure the eltfttion of school boards in

rural districts; to secure the compulsory
attendance at schools of all children of school
age; and that the provisions relating to school
fees be modified. Without very precisely
pledging himself to anything, the ViCE-
PRESIDENT appeared to intimate that next
year he will introduce modifications of the
Act, with a view to these three points. "I
admit," he said, "the difficulty raised, and I
think that when we pass one general com-
pulsory law we may try whether we cannot
obtain a substitute for the two clauses which
would meet the object we have in view. But
I am persuaded it is impossible to do so this
year, and I think nothing would help the
question so much as the experiment being tried
by the School Board of London. They seemed to
have met the matter practically, and I think from
their experience and the experience of other
boards we shall ascertain how the difficulty is to
be met. In candour I must add, that I could
never consent to any alteration which would
break down what I considtz a principle of
justice, namely, that you must give to the
parent, prevented by poverty thorn sending
his children to school, the power of choosing
which he will send his children to. I shall
be told that there is a difficulty in defending
this principle while you enforce compulsory
attendance in country districts, where there is
only one school. That, however, we have
nothing to do with here. My object is not
to give denominational education, nor to pre-
vent it. My object is to secure secular educa-
tion, and give as much freedom as possible
with regard to religious education." This is
well so far as it goes, but not enough to in-
duce the objectors, after past experience, to
lay down their arms and resume the pipe of
peace.

HOW TO SAVE THE COUNTRY AND
PRESERVE THE THRONE.

WE think we may say that all good men
rejoiced over the recovery of the PRINCE of
WALES, and we imagine we may add
that most sensible people will be heartily glad
that the Thanksgiving is a thing of the past.
It was painful when a mother, a wife, and
children were plunged into anxiety and fear
for the life of a son, a husband, and a father.
And over and above the natural sympathy
with those who thus suffered, the nation no
doubt very sincerely wished the" reeoiery of
the Heir-Apparent.
But surely all this, and ten times as much,
in the way of sympathy, sorrow, or 'rejoicing,
might be expressed soberly and decently, and
without unseemly and illogical reference to
principles of Government or political party
mano3uvres. We wish we could say that the
nauseating twaddle to which we refer was
confined to one or two of our newspapers, or
that we could eompensate ourselves by pointing
to oven one leading journal in whose columns
anything manly or sensible was to be found.
The whole thing was, an outpouring of cant
and rubbish, histrionic blubber, gushings of
tears, snufflings of sighs, strained swellings
of loyal breasts, and hysterical outbursts of
silly satisfaction. The moralisings, too, were
remarkable. AU the bad taste in calico and
red flannel was declared to be the result of an
intense devotion to the principle of Royalty;
whilst the crowding and crushing in the streets
betokened an allegiance to the throne which
nothing could shake.
We have no disposition to moralise this
display in an adverse sense, thouoh a great
deal might be said on popular shows, from
the Derby-day at Epsom to a hanging day at
the Old Bailey; or, from the procession of the
'great Hindoo idol to the exhibition of the
holy coat at Troves. Disregarding all this,
however, we believe there was much sound
loyalty in the Thanksgiving display, much
personal affection for the QUEEN as a woman,
as well as for the Throne as an institution. We
had no need of the display of the 27th to con-
vince us that the form of Government we have
is preferred to any other by the great majority
of the people of England. Babecause we believe
this we are not disposed to scream out insanely
like the Standard, or clap our wings and crow,
like our clever contemporaries,as if the millennial
sun had shot his first shafts above the horizon.
The Standard exclaims "We have heard a
great deal of late of the expense of monarchy.
not that expense more than justified by the

spectacle of yesterday P' We do not see what
the two things have to do with each other.
The speetacle was grand enough in its way,
but monarchy may be too expensive never.
theless ; so may bread, or coals, or mutton.
A monarchy may be the best thing in the
world, but there is no use in spending more on
it than is needful..

"What Republic on earth," the Standan/
asks, " could inspire in its people so
genuine and hearty
.a feeling of love
for itself as this ' demonstration 'proves to
exist in the English ' nation for its
Sovereign ? '' The question was not a pr udent
one to put. There was a great crowd, and the
windows along the route were decorated, and
their proprietors sold seats in them and possi-
bly turned a Pretty penny. But the Standard
must not forget, and if it is disposed to do so
the Alabama claims may remind it, that in a
Republic) on the other side of the Atlantic, in
defence of, law, hundreds of thousands of
citizens gave their dearest and best to the,
grave, scores of thousands left their quiet em-
ployments and their happy homes, and gave
their lives ass sacrifice to preserve the unity
and greatness of their native laud. Compari-
sons are proverbially odious, and we therefore
shall not compare. the devoted heroes of tho
young Republic of the West, who went in
crowds to their graves, to the sight-seers, or
even to the sincere elturoh-goers of that day;
but
,we consider it due to truth to say that
whatever We may think of the loyalty of the
shopkeepers in Fleet-street and the Strand, or
the crowds who flocked to ace the speetacle of
the 27th, we cannot place them very far
above the citizens of the "United States in
patriotic devotion to national law and national
life.

Of course it was right and fitting enough
that the press should give it heavy and hot to
SIR CIIARLEB DUKE and GEORGE ODUER
Anything such persons can do at the Hole-in-
the-Wall or elsewhere, must be very poor and
common-place compared with the Thanks-
givingdisplay. But after all has been
said, we must come back to the fad that
common sense is common sense," and that
loyalty has its lures as well as extreme
radicalism, nobody can doubt who has glanced
during tho past week at the columns of our
daily and weekly papers. What can be finer
in its way as a specimen of "midsummer mad.
ness " than the following " clipped" from our
respectable contemporary, the Standard, the
day after the procession :—" Let us hope that
the moral of yesterday's ceremonial will not be
lost; that in future we shall have more
frequent opportunities of demonstrating the
popular enthusiasm for Royalty; that QUEEN
and people may know more of each other. It
is only thus that we can most effectually meet
all dangers, domestic and foreign, that we can
keep together that great Empire, of which the
Throne is the 'cement and the corner stone,
that our SOVEREIGN will reign in greatest
happiness and serenity—

"Broad-based upon her people's will,
And compassed by the inviolate sea."

It would be diffioult to imagine anything
finer in its way than this, or more worthy of
the organ of the great Conservative party who
claim to possess a monopoly of the loyalty of
the country. It has just one drawback, how-
ever, as when examined narrowly, it has all
the appearance of a covert satire on the in-
stitution it ostensibly lauds. Extremes we
know meet, and it is for that reason perhaps
that this "clipping" from the Standard looks
so much like a sly thrust made at monarchy
through the "fob-in-the-Wall." According to
this, in its true reading, the Throne is to find
ita most effectual strength in red baize, bunt-
ing, and gay processions. "is is only this
we can most effectually
meet all dangers, do..
mestio and foreign." What a happy discovery
National defence cheap as an old song
processions once a year, once a month perhaps,
once a week if need be, every day should any
foreign enemy make his appearance off our
coasts ; cheap too, as the old Romans bought
the loyalty of the crowd by adding bread.
We wiser in our generation lay nothing about
the more costly part of the bribe. When
NAPOLEON approached Rome the POP I: rnado a
procession with his priests, monks, and holy
relics. It Was a very imposing sight, and the

official journals of the day described it in
glowing terms, very much like those- employed
by our journals now. It did not answer, but
that was BoLt.Lotie's fault, who unfortunately
had. a habit,of laughing at such things. How-
ever, go idea suggested . by: our contemporary
is a goed one, and ought to be tried. If it
does not a-nswer, we may try to see what
virtue there is in an honest, economic, and
wise government; in the comfort and content-
ment of the maises of the people; and in all
those other agencies believed in by sensible
and liberal men. Shows are good enough in
their way, and are capital things. for the news-
papers; but wise laws which secure the liberty,
and increase the happiness of the masscs of the
people are, we venture to say, better; but at
the present moment, and until our extra loyal
people have returned to their senses, we do not
absolutely insist on this.

MR. AYRTON ON HIS HIGH HORSE.I

Tun answer given by Mr. AYRTON to Sir
Wurnin LAWSON as to the Hyde Park meet-
ing of last Sunday, was quite unique in its
way. Tho question was whether the meeting
about to be held was to be permitted or pre-
vented,. and the proper answer should have
been negative or affirmative. And if Mr.
Ayrton Wag not Commissioner of Works, and
if his imagination Was not disturbed by a too
sublime sense of the duties belonging to his
office, he would very likely have answered the
question in the plain and simple language of
every day life. He would have said that it
was the intention of the Government to pre-
vent the meeting, or that it was not the inten-
tion of the Government to do so; or that he
had not been informed what it was the inten-

With what copiousness ho would have die-

kind of attention to reason, it was comfort-
ing for the country to know that what he and
other official persons Wore seeking to' do in

, -

parks, should, on the first opportunity, relioyo

pations.

The conduct of the. Finance M

Further, preparations are said to be making
for the evacuation ,of . the Vatican, and even
Cardinal ANTONELLI is spoken of as begin-
ning to pack up and make ready for departure.
It is by no means certain, however, whether
the POPE will go with him, or he with the
POPE. • But the thieves falling, out affords a

But the most remarkable feature in the
week's news 'from. France is the speech of
M, T WAIN, the working man, and prominent

com-

.against, the spirit of solidarity among the,

M. ToLuN, made another, point before he

sary
.betwetu workman and master. The great

lishing anything like a satisfactory equality.
As for the liberty of association, it wa's a grave

articles.text:
A NEW MODE OF THROWING OUT

BILLS.

THE House of Lords is indebted to the
Marquis of SALISBURY for the suggestion of a
short method with popular Bills. .He ventured
to suggest, that great advantage would arise
from their lordships examining subjects before-
hand by moans of Select Committees, or from

the simultaneous introduction of measures into
both Houses. He feared, however, that that
proposal was of too revolutionary a character
for the noble EARL to assent to, at least until
he had had time to recover from the shook;
but such a plan would enable their lordships to
consider Bills with more deliberate care and
attention. Earl GREY said that so exceedingly
unsatisfactory was the present system
that
legislation of a highly desirable character was
postponed from year to year, and what:was
actually done, was done in so confused and un-
workmanlike a manner, that an Act rarely •
passed which did not require a Bill the next
year or the year after to correct its obvious
guilders. The House of Commons ahoitia
adopt a standing order to
_the effect that a Bill
passed late in the Session should be held over
till the next year, and then be revived and
sent up to their' lordships iipon a single vote,
taken without debate. Lord REDESDALE,
however, did not think there was any defi-
ciency of legislation. There was plenty of it;
he only wished it was better. He had no
objection to see Bills thrown out; quite the
contrary. A rejected measure generally
proved a better one when it reappeared. It
must be borne in mind, Inwever, said Earl
GRANVILLE, that to introduce a Bill into their
Lordships' House involved the risk of its being
lost without having received that amount of
ventilation which might be desirable. As
regarded the Mines Bill, it was true that many
of their lordships were interested in it as pro-
prietors, and many more were interested in 1
the Welfare of the workmen; but the Hens°
of COmmohs was in both respects a more
representative body.

articles.title: INTERNATIONAL AR AITRATION.
articles.text:
INTERNATIONAL AR AITRATION.

MR. RICHARD'S MOTION.

Notwithstanding the unexpected turn which the
indirect claims of the United States have given to
the question of arbitration, it is the intention of
Mr. H. Richard, ALP., to proceed with the motion
of wliich ho has given notice in the House of
Commons. He feels that; even if this particular
arbitration should fall through, it will not prove
the impracticable character of the proposals made
for establishing a general And permanent system of
International Arbitration. It will prove exactly
the reverse. It will prove the urgent and crying
need that exists for a High Court of Nations ao a
permanent impartial tribunal, to decide upon and
apply the international laws previously settled and
agreed to by a General Congress of representatives
of the various countries. What the advocates of a
stipulated and prearranged system of arbitration
say is this, that wars most frequently become
inevitable between nations, not because the orginal
point of difference is incapable of a paeifie solu-
tion, but because those differences become infl timed
by angry recriminations and: the clamorous outeliei
of popular passion. When all the parties to the
quarrel have becoraa thus compromised and ex-
asperated, it is no wonder if there is difficulty,
even by means of a friendly arbitration La corn

posing the difference. It is believed, and has long
been advocated by the friends of peace, that this
evil may to a great extent be avoided by first
agreeing to certain general rules of international
law, and then establishing some permanent form of
international jurisdiction, to which the disputes of
States may be referred befere the original difficulty
has become complicated and aggravated by excited
feeling and points of, what is called, national
honour. And does not the American ease furnish
a striking illustration of these remarks? If there
had been in the first instance something like a
well-defined and generally-accepted law On the
duties of neutrals as to equipping and sending
forth ships from their ports, it is in the highest
degree improbable that the difficulty would have
arisen at all; and if it had arisen, and there had
existed such an International Tribunal as that for
which the Peace Society pleads, to which the
question could have been referred, the difficulty
would have been solved at once, before men's
minds had been disturbed and inflamed by mutual
recriminations.

THE MEMORANDUM
MITCHELL ON THE CHINA TRADE
IN 1852, REFERRED TO IN MR.'
CROMPTON'S
.ARTICLE.

"During two years of uninterrupted residence
in this country, in three separate provinces, and
after a most careful observation of the very fact
I am now about to enlarge upon, I can safely
aver that, with the exception of our own domestics,
I have never. yet seen a Chinaman wearing a
garment of our long-cloth who had to get his daily
bread by his daily labour. No working Chinarnan
can afford to put on a now coat, which shall not
last him at least three years, and stand the wear
and tear of the roughest drudgery during that
period. Now a garment of that description must
contain at least three times the weight of raw
cotton which we put into the heaviest goods we
export to China. No doubt we could supply this
country with goods as heavy; but whether we
could do so as cheaply as they can produce them
for themselves, will presently appear.
"The best made of illustrating the question will
be by a single example taken from the province
with which I am best acquainted—that of Fuh-
Kien ; and I would beg to direct the particular
attention of the Board of Trade to the beautiful
and simple economy of it; an economy which
renders the system literally impregnable
against all the Assaults of competition. It is, of
course, understood that the different provinces of
China yield different products according to their
respective soils and climate, and that the trade
of the country with itself consists chiefly in the
interchange of those productions. The Northern
provinces yield cotton amongst other products in
great abundance. The Southern, rice, sugar,
fruits, drugs, dyes, and teas. Now the Full-
Kien farmer, among his other crops, raises
a certain proportion of sugar. This he disposes
of in the spring to a trader at the nearest sea-
port, who ships it to Tien-tsin, or some other
Northern port, during the southerly monsoon,
undertaking to pay the farmer for it, part in
money and part in Northern cotton, when his
junk returns, say in four to six months. In the
autumn the farmer receives his returns, one por-
tion of which consists of cotton, which he works
up as follows: When the harvest is gathered, all
hands in the farmhouse, young and old together,
, turn to carding, spinning, and weaving this
cotton; and out of this home-spun stuff, a heavy
and durable material, adapted to the rough hand-
, ling it has to go through for two or three years,
they clothe themselves, and the surplus they carry
to the narest town, whore the shop-keeper buys
it for the use of the population of 'the towns and
the boat people on the rivers. Of this home-spun
stuff, nine out of, every ten human beings in this
country are clothed; the manufacture vary-
ing in quality from the coarsest dungarn
to the finest flanking, all produced in the
farmhouses, and costing the producer literally
nothing beyond the value of the raw material, or
rather of the sugar which he exchanged for it, the
produce of his own husbandry. The Full-Men
farmer is thus not merely, a farmer, but an agri-
culturist and manufacturer in one. lie produces
this cloth literally for nothing beyond the cost
of the raw material; he produces it, as has been
shown, under his own roof-tree, by the hands of
his women and farm servants; it costs neither
extra labour nor extra time. Ile keeps his
domestics spinning and weaving while his crops
are growing, and after they are harvested, during
rainy weather, when out-door labour cannot be
pursued. . . , In 1844 I dent musters of
this native cloth of every quality home to Eng-
land, and my correspondents assured me they
could not produce it in Manchester at the rates
quoted, ratioh less lay it down bore. The unceas-
ing industry of this people is their substitute for
steam-power ; and, coupled with their swarming
numbers, is more than a match for it. . . . .
"We bring the Chinese nothing that is really
popular amongst them„ except our opium. Opium
is the open sesame' to their stony hearts, and
woo betide our trade the day we meddle with it,
to its injury. As fast as the Company,
will pro
duce opium, the Cliiiguie will consume it.

articles.title: RECLAIMED LAND ON THE THAMES EMBANKMENT.
articles.text:
RECLAIMED LAND ON THE THAMES
EMBANKMENT.

On Monday a special meeting of the Metro-
politan Board of Works, Colonel Hogg,
M.P., in the chair, was held at the office in
Spring-gardens, for the consideration of a
letter from the Hon. Charles A. Gore, one of
the Commissioners of Woods, Forests, and
Land Revenues, on the subject of land re-
claimed. in the construction of the Victoria
Embankment. The communication, which is
of some length sets forth that the ground in
question was about two acres and
,a half in
extent, and lies between the Embankment
roadway and that portion of Crown property
which extends from Whitehall-gardens to
Whitehall-place, and which belonged to the
Crown before the .Etnbankment was made.
The select committee of the House of Com-
mons recommended that the land should be
appropriated as a garden for the use of the
public, at a rental calculated after the rate
paid for the adjoining portions of land re-
claimed and appropriated by the Act of 1862,
to the Crown tenants, at the instance of the
Commissioners of Woods and Forests, and
that such land be offered upon lease to the
Metropolitan Board of Works at a rental cal-
culated aforesaid. Mr. Gore submitted the
following proposition: "The Crown to sell the
two acres of land to the Board for such a sum
as shall represent the estimated loss which
will be sustained by the Crown and the public
at large, if the proposition in the report of the
select committee, as to the dedication of the
land in question as a publio garden is
adopted, in lieu of the proposed appropria.
tion ; the amount to be paid to be settled by
arbitration."

Dr. Brewer, M.P., moved, and Mr. Sawyer
seconded, a resolution as follows :---
" That the letter of Mr. Charles Gore be re-
ferred'to the Works and General Purposes Com-
mittee for consideration and report, and that an
instruction be given to the committee to adhere to
the principle of negotiation recommended by the
select committee of the House of Commons."

After a few observations from Mr. Richard-
son to the effect that, unless the Board
obtained the fee-simple of the land, they
would have to go into the matter over again,
Mr. Newton declared that the proposition
could not be entertained, though the Board
was willing to negotiate on the basis of the
select committee's report, and he moved as an
amendment:— t

"That, in the present state of the question
before Parliament, the Board think it bettor to
defer entering into the consideration of tho pro-
posals of Mr. Gore with reference to the Thames
Embankment land until Parliament has decided
upon the question."

After some discussion, the amendment was
passed by lo votes to 2.
Mr. Turner then moved a second amend-
ment to the effect that the Board did not
deem it proper to entertain the proposals con-
tained in Mr. Gore's letter; and this having
been seconded by Mr. Freeman, was carried
unanimously.
Some further business was transacted, and
the sitting was adjourned.'

articles.title: Alit. BRIGHT ON THE INCOME TAX.
articles.text:
Alit. BRIGHT ON THE INCOME TAX.

A deputation from the Birmingham Anti-
Income Tax Association have had an inter-
view with the Chancellor of the Exchequer,
to represent their views. Mr. Bright was in-
vited with the other borough members to join
the deputation, and in reply he has sent the
following letter to the Honorary Secretary to
the movement :

" Rochdale' March 4, 1872.
"Dear Sir,—l regret to say that I shall not be
able to be in town on Wednesday, and therefore I
cannot take part in the proposed deputation to the
Chancellor of the Exchequer. There is little real
Aifference of opinion as to the odious and unfair
character of the income tax; but it is not easy to
see where the money is to be obtained which now
comes from that tax. I see no chance of its
abolition except in a lessened expenditure, and at
present there seems no probability of the creation
of a political party resolved to lessen the public
expenditure, and adopting that policy as the one
great article of its creed. Ido not believe in
Governments that cannot govern without taking
seventy milliens every year from the industry of
the nation, and I hope the time will come when no
such Government will be permitted to exist. For
myself I should be ready to vote for such reduction
of expenditure as would enable the Chancellor of
the Exchequer to remove the income tax or to
abolish the taxes which add so greatly to the price
of tea, coffee, and sugar.—l am, truly yours,
" 414fi Liftwur.
"To U. W. Plant, Esq."

articles.title: FORS CLAVIGERA. LETTER THE FOURTEENTH." BY JOHN RusicrN, LL.D.
articles.text:
FORS CLAVIGERA. LETTER THE
FOURTEENTH."
BY JOHN RusicrN, LL.D.

Mr. Ruskin in this letter gives some borne
thrusts to, and asks a few difficult questions
to answer of, the workmen and labourers oC
Great Britain. The following extracts are
curious—written, too, in Mr. Ruskin's quaint
style :
Are you ready even now, in the height of your
morality, to give back India to the Brahmins and
their cows or Australia to her aborigines tind
their apes P You are ready P Well, my Christian
friends, it does one's heart good to hear it, pro-
viding only you are quite sure you know what
you are about. "Let him that stole steal no
more, but rather let him labour." You are verily
willing to accept that alternative? I inquire
anxiously, because I see that your Under• Secre-
tary of State for India, Mr. Grant Duff, proposes
to you in his speech at Elgin, not at all as the
first object of your lives to be honest; but, as the
first, to be rich, and the second to be intelligent;
now when you have become all rich and intelli-
gent, how do you mean to live? Mr. Grant Duff,
of course, means by being rich that you are each
to have two powdered footmen—but then who are
to be the footmen now that we mustn't have
blacks? and granting you all the intelligence in
the world on the most important subjects—the
spots on the sun, or the nodes of the moon, as
aforesaid, will that help you to get your dinner,
unless you steal it in the old fashion? The sub-
ject is, indeed, discussed with closer definition than
by Mr. Grant Duff by Mr. William Riddle, C.E.,
the authority I quoted to you for taking property
"under controul."

Than Mr. Ruskin gives the following curious
quotation from what Mr. Riddle says in an
article entitled" The Simple and only Remedy
for the Wants of Nations'

"These are all-in-all. What all nations want,
Sir, are—l, shelter; 2, food ;3, clothes ;4,
warmth; 5, cleanliness; 6, health; 7, love; 8,
beauty. These are only to be got in one way; I
will state it. An international Congress must
make a number of steam engines or use those now
made, and taking all property under its control
(I fearlessly state it), must roll off iron and glass
for buildings to shelter hundreds of millions of
people.-2. Must, by such engines, make steam
apparatus to plough immense plains of wheat,
where steam has elbow room abroad; must
make engines to grind it on an enormous scale,
first fetching it in flat-bottomed ships, made of
simple form, larger than the Groat Eastern, and
of simple form of plates, machine-fastened; must
bake it by machine ovens commensurate.-3.
Machine looms must work unattended night and
day, rolling off textile yarns and fabrics; and
machines must make clothes, just as envelopes are
knocked off.-4. Machinery must do laundress'
work—iron and mangling; and, in a word, our
labour must give place to machinery', laid down in
gigantic factories, on common-sense principles, by
an international leverage. This is the education
you must inculcate. Then man will be at last
emancipated. All else is utter bosh, and I will
prove it so when and wherever I can get the
means to lecture. Thum( RIDDLE, C.E.
South Lambeth.

" Unfortunately," adds Mr. Ruskin, "till these
moans can be obtained (may it be soon) it remains
unriddled to us on what principles of interna-
tional leverage' the love and beauty are to be
provided ;,but the point I wish you mainly to
notice is, that for this general emancipation and
elbow room for men and steam, you are still re-
quired to find immense plains of wheat abroad.'
Is it not probable that these immense plains May
belong to somebody 'abroad' already P"
Fur the rest we must refer our readers to the
clever fourteenth letter of Mr. Ruskin.

articles.title: LABOUR REPRESENTATION LEAGUE.
articles.text:
LABOUR REPRESENTATION LEAGUE.

On Friday night in the large hall of the
German club, Foley-street, the members of
the above league hold their anniversary festi-
val. Mr. U. M. Latham, President of the
League, occupied the chair, and in giving the
toast of the Queen, remarked thatwhile anxious
to assert the principle of popular sovereignty,
the league could not ailed to ignore the gene-
ral will of the nation. Queen Victoria
occupying the throne by the consent of the
majority of the nation, the members of tkis.
league could not but confess their admiration
of her personal character and virtues.
"The People, the Source of• all Legitimate
Power," was given, the Chairman endeavour-
ing to show by,the history of recant legislation
that the masses of the people were acquiring
daily more political power. Mr. Lloyd Jones,
Mr. G. Potter, and Mr. Magee Pratt respbnded
to the sentiment, the first-named gentleman
endorsing most fully the Chairman's idea that
the power of the people was growing daily. It
was only by the pressure of public opinion, he
argued, that the politica.] power had been
gained which the people now possessed, and he
advised an intelligent use of that power in
order to secure its extension.

The next toast was "Success to the Labour
Representation League," in proposing which
the Chairman argued that they must, in seek-
ing the reforms which were on their programme,
co-operate heartily and earnestly, oven though
on some points they might differ, with the
Liberal party. Mr. Mottershead, Mr. Boon,
and Mr. Ryans responded to the toast. Several
other toasts were given and responded to, and
during the evening there was some excellent
singing.

articles.title: LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.
articles.text:
LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

On Wednesday, at the fortnightly meeting
of this Board, Lord Lawrence in the chair,
The Rev. Canon Miller gave notice that he
would move at the next meeting that the
resolution passed in December, 1870, deoiding
that no salaries be given to the chairman and
the vice-chairman of the Board be rescinded
Mr. E. H. Currie moved,

"That a letter be addressed to the managers or
trustees of the public elementary schools in the
metropolis, urging upon them to consider the adven
tages of placing their schools under the School Board,
and suggesting that application be made to the
members for their division for any necessary
explanations; also that a letter explanatory of the
conditions on which schools are now being taken
over by the Board be prepared by the works Coolmittee."

The object which Mr. Currie had in view
was to turn to the best advantage the
resources of existing schools previous to the
Board commencing to incur the cost of
establishing new schools. He found that
there were 860 public elementary schools in
the metropolis, capable of accommodating
273,000, and that there were as many
as over
90,000 vacant seats in those schools. Tftere
was accommodation for 90,000 children, which
was not availed of. This represented a
capital of half a million of money. To those
schools the government contributed a large
sum of money every year. Surely this
immense accommodation, which was waiting
to be made use of, ought not to be allowed to
remain idle.

Mr. Crossman seconded the proposition.
The Yen. J. Mee moved "the previous
question," which, it is well-known, means
that the quastion should be shelved. In
opinion, if the Board passed Mr. Currie 's
motion they would violate the spirit of the
Act which they were called upon to carry out.
Up to the present the Board had been merely.
theorising. They had not as yet built one
single school. Would it not be better to
delay anything in the shape of what Mr. Currie
desired till they had some practical results of
what the Board had already done? It was
reite• possible that the existing denomina'
tional schools would prove more acceptable to
the people than the schools which the Board
contemplated erecting (hear, hear).
Mr. Lafone seconded the amendment, and
urged the inadvisability of doing anything
which would cripple voluntary effort. Ho
believed Mr. Currie's motion would have that
effect. He therefore was opposed to it.
The discussion was continued by the Rev.
B. Waugh, and Mr. Hepworth Dixon, who
supported the original motion; the Rev. Pre-
bendary Thorold, who opposed it; the Rev.
J. A. Picton, who sympathised with the
object which Mr. Currie had in view,
but thought the motion went too far,
and would therefore oppose it; Miss Davis,
who supported it; Mr. 'Pearce, who urged
the advisability of having nothing to do with
the question at present, and reminded the
Board that they had already a "terrible amount
of work" on hand which more urgently re-
quired the attention of the Board; and Mr.
Currie, who complained that his motion had
been misrepresented, and withdrew it in com-
pliance with what appeared to be the feeling
of the Board.

Mr. Chas. Reed, M.P., moved the adoption of
recommendations of the works committee relating
to the purchase of various pieces of ground on
which schools are to be built, in Old Ford,
Hackney, Tooting, Graveney, Lambeth, and
Haggerston, and for the renting of various
schools in Xornsey-road, Caledonian-road, Water,
100-road, Stepney, East India•road, Bromley-by
Bow, Drury-lane, and other places.
The motion was agreed to nem. con.
A long discussion took place as to what the
dimensions of the new class-rooms should be.
It was agreed that nine square feet should be
allowed to each child, and that no class-room
should be less than 300 superficial feet. It
was understood this decision referred only to
the three or four sohools about to be constructed,
and that the general question will be discussed
at some future period.
On the motion of Mr. MiGregor, Mr. John
Noble, of the Woolwich Arsenal Schools, was
appointed an inspector under the Board,at a
salary of £3OO a year.
In reply to a question put by the Rev. jno.
Rodgers, it was stated by Mr. Meregor, that
there was no truth in a report which had got
abroad that two of the candidates for the
office had been rejected on the ground that
their signatures had been attached to .a ,me-
morial presented to the Board. That fact
might have affected some individual members
of the committee, but certainly not the com-
mittee as a whole.

Mr. Lueraft thought that the appointment
of such officers should not be left altogether to
any committee (hear, hear).
On the motion of Mr. Reed, M.P., a Mr. W.
Hetherington was appointed a superintendent
of visitors and clerk of the divutional oom-
mittee of visitors,
at a salary of £l5O a year.
And on the motion of Mr. Buxton Lieut.
Colonel Vivian was appointed a superintendent
for Tower Hamlets, at £2OO a year.
The Board adjournod shortly aftei six
o'clock.

articles.title: INTERNATIONAL.
articles.text:
THE INTERNATIONAL.

From the reports of the general council, we
gather that the International is as active as
ever. On the occasion of the last two sittings
the following announcements were made :
A new organ of the association is to appear 011
the Ist of March, the title to be the Inter-
national; office, 7, Rod Lion-court. New
branches have been formed in Dundee, and at
Hinckley, in Leicestershire, and are in course
of formation in Woolwich and Sunderland.
The secretary for France announced that the
association had been reorganised in Algeria,
and that the movement was extending rapidly
in that colony. A report had been received
from the Federal Council of North America,
from which it appeared that the progress in
the States had been very great indeed. There
are now forty-one sections in active operation.
Citizen Jung proposed "that a committee be
appointed to arrange a meeting to celebrate
the revolution of the 18th of March." "It
was the first success of the workmen, and
showed that the working classes were quite
able to govern themselves." The resolution
was carried unanimously, and it was decided
that all bodies of working men should co-
operate with the committee in furtherance of
this purpose. It was further announced that
"The Society of Freedom" of Vienna had
been dissolved upon the plea that it was in
correspondence .with the Socialist movement
in the rest of Europe. In Hungary the
workmen were being persecuted and prevented
from holding meetings by a commissary of
the police. The Madrid section of the as-
sociation has issued a manifesto with reference
.to the veto upon public meeting and free
speech of the International in Spain, declaring
that if the members were not allowed to meet
peaceably, they would resort to arms in
defence of their rights. From Switzerland '
the news was of an exciting nature. The
house of Citizen Ontino, late editor of the
Egalite, had been searched on the demand of
the Russian police, the plea being a charge of
forgery. The matter ended in no papers
being found of a.compremising character, and
a proper apology was made to Citizen Ontine.
This conduct on the part of the Russian
Government is denounced by a declaration of
the general council. The Irish section of the
International met at the Grapes, Great Marl-
borough-street, on the 18th inst., upon which
occasion the secretary for Ireland, Mr.
M‘Donnell, made some very business-like
remarks. He particularly urged the duty of
temperance, and hoped that no member would
be admitted of intemperate habits. These
observations, we are glad to find, were heartily
applauded. Mr. J. Murphy discoursed upon
the aims of the International, and the beneilt
to accrue to Ireland from a connection with
it. It was proposed to form sections at
Rotherhithe and Deptford. From these reports
it will be seen that the International is
rapidly adding to the number of its members
both at home and abroad.—P(/// Ga:eite.

At last, however, everything had been de-

1,900 would receive something in the shape of

Patterson thought that he was justified in
averring that the late working men's exhibi-

that
has been hold. Mr. Newton of the Mint,
stated that he had some difilou,
lty in making

intendant of the coining department, had
gone to much trouble in the matter. After the
distribution of prizes a vote of thanks was

articles.text:
lIIPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS,-THURSDAY.

The motion of Sir M. H. Beach to refer- the
Ballot Bill and the Corrupt Practices Bill "to
the same Committee" was denounced by Sir
Geo. Grey as inappropriate, and indeed as
.inconsistent, with the orders of the House,
but nevertheless it led to a long discussion.
Mr. Fawcett, in his firmest language, gave
his support to the proposal; and declared that
a Ballot Bill was not worth having unless it
was associated with a measure for the greven-
tion of corrupt practices.
In vain Lord John Ma.nners,,asked from Mr.
Forster an: assurance that he would not
report this measure until the Corrupt Practices
Bill had reached a similar stage. All that he
could elicit from the right hon. gentleman was
that the Government intended, if possible, to
pass both Bills, and would take the Cor-
rupt Practices Bill in Committee immediately
after the Ballot Bill.
Mr. F. S. Powell, the new Conservative
member for North-west Yorkshire, founding
himself upon American, and especially Cali-
fornian experience' warmly supported the
introduction of the Ballot.
After a protracted discussion, Mr. Gladstone,
about ten o'clock, offered to incorporate with
the Ballot Bill the second and third clauses
of the Corrupt Practices Bill, dealing with
personation and the striking off of votes for
bribery or intimidation, and this overture
being recognised by Mr. Disraeli as fair and
honourable, the amendment of the hon.
baronet the member for Gloucestershire was
negatived without a division, and the House
proceeded to the consideration of
Mr. Cavendish Bentinck's proposal, that
they should in their divisions vote by ballot.
This amendment the hon. member moved in a
speech which Mr. Forster described as so
jocose that it called for no reply.
Mr. G. H. Bentinek most indignantly pro-
tested against the attribution of humour to his
relative, and provoked a conflict with the
Speaker by denouncing the amount of corrup-
tion and intimidation which prevailed within
the walls of Parliament itself. This was
more than the Speaker could permit; and the
member for Norfolk was obliged to confine his
observations to past Houses of Commons, omit-
ting from censure th at in which heis now sitting.
The amendment was negatived without a
division, and the House went into Committee.
Immediately thereupon Mr. C. Boutin*
moved the postponement of the first clause.
This time he took the sense of the House, and
was handsomely beaten by a majority of 73-
218 to 145. _ . _

-- ---
In Committee there was a good deal of dis-
cussion upon an amendment proposed by Mr.
Goldney upon the first clause, and when this
had been disposed of progress was reported.
Soon afterwards the House adjourned.

articles.title: HOUSE OF COMMON 5.7-FRIDAY.
articles.text:
HOUSE OF COMMON 5.7-FRIDAY.

In the Commons, Sir R. Palmer's proposal
for the establishment in London of a Central
School of Law, for the scientific education of
barristers and attorneys in the principles of
jurisprudence, and the practice of their profes-
sion was supported by Mr. 0. Morgan, and
produced a good deal of discussion.
Speaking on the part of the Government,
the Attorney-General denied that there was
any necessity to undertake the teaching of
law, any more than that of medicine or any
other profession. He maintained that all
that was wanted was a strict examination,
and that for this purpose the powers already
possessed and exercised by the Inns of Court
were amply sufileient.
The resolution was ultimately negatived by
116 to 103, and soon afterwards the House
adjourned. '

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY.
The Marquis. of Clanrioarde moved in the
House of Lords for copies of the instructions
under which Captain Tyler was authorised to
collect information with respect to the finan-
cial condition of the Irish railways. The Earl
of Dufferin replied that there were no instruc-
tions or reports to produce. Captain Tyler had
bet% "permitted, rather than authorised," to
ascertain from persons connected with Irish
railways, "what, in their opinion, were the
terms on which those undertakings might be
bought."
A. conversation on the state of business was
opened by the Duke of Itiohmond, who com-
plained that their Lordships had nothing to
do, whilst the House of Commons was busy.
Earl Granville said that several Irish bills
would be initiated in the House of Lords
before Easter ; and Viscount Halifax
added that the proper function of the
House of Lords was the revision and
not the initiation, of bills. Lord West-
bury elicited from the Lord Chancellor that he
intends shortly to introduce two bills, one for
the creation of a High Court of Judicature,
and
.the other for the establishment of a Court
oflinal Appeal, The House then adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.-11oNnkr.
In the House of Commons, before the Army
Estimates were reached Ministers were called
upon to reply to several important questions.
Mr, Bowring asked the Premier, with.

reference to the correspondence relating to
the ex-Governor of Jamatealately laid upon the
table, whether it was his intention to submit a
vote for the repayment to General Eyre of the
expenses incurred by him in respect of legal
proceedings against him, an estimate for which,
amounting to £4,133, was laid upon the table
by the Government on the 28th July last,
but subsequently withdrawn by them.
Mr. Gladstone said that the Government,
considered themselves bound by the cor-
respondence which bad taken place to re-
introduce the estimate.

In reply to Mr. Hussey • Vivian Lord
Enfield detailed the ill-success which had
attended the efforts of the Foreign Office to
bring to justice the murderer of a British
subject in Spain. The Spanish authorities
appear to have connived at a gross evasion
of justice.
Mr. W. E. Forster gave some particulars
of the establishment of schools by school
boards.

Lord Enfield stated the result of' the in-
quiries which had been made with respect to
the deportation of French political offenders.
Lord Lyons has been instructed to present a
strong remonstrance at Versailles.
Mr. Lowe stated, in answer to Mr. Barnett
and Colonel Tomline, that the mint had.
already overtaken the demand for silver coin.
The House then went into Committee of
Supply, and Mr. Cardwell moved a vote of
133,619 men for the land forces. Mr. Ilolms
moved the reduction of the vote by 2C,000
men, and Mr. Muntz seconded the amendment.
The subject was discussed at very great
length, and, was adjourned.

articles.title: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.
articles.text:
HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.

The Irish Church Act Amendment Bill and
the Irish Parks Bills were both read a second
time.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MESDIY.

The main topic of discussion was the opera-
tion of the Education Act.
Mr. Dixon moved a series of resolutions
declaring that the provisions of that statute
were defective and unsatisfactory, and sup-
ported his raotion•in a speech in which he
declared that while the Act was under discus-
sion the Nonconformists were always out-
voted, and demanded that all the cobwebs of a
supposed compromise should be swept away.
He dwelt forcibly upon the deficiencies of the
denominational system, the want of funds, the
insufficient payment of masters, and the in-
sufficiency of pupil teachers. The hon. gentle-
man was sharp upon the Conservative party
and the Church of England for the opposition
which they had offered to the constitution of
School Boards; and demanded a complete
separation of secular and religious edueation,
which, he asserted, would ensure complete har-
mony among Men of all religions. His refer-
ence to the great work which Mr. Forster—
whom he expressly stated he had no desire to
turn out of office—had accomplished, was
cheered from both sides of the House.

Mr. H. Richard, in seconding the motion, I
referred to the tumultuous cheering which the
Vice-President of the Council generally elicited
from the Opposition benches, and described
this as "the fish for which the right hon.
gentleman was generally angling." He coin-
plained of the want of Nonconformist
inspectors, and quoted two or three books
which had been used in sohools to show that
the teaching of the Established Church was
opposed to Protestantism ; but Mr. W. H.
Smith (interrupting) pointed out that one of
these books was issued by a firm of Roman
Catholic publishers.
Mr. W. E. Forster rose before seven o'clock,
and spoke for nearly an hour and a half.
There was no want of ;cheering in the course of
his address, but it came mainly from the Oppo-
sition benches. From his own side of the
House the expressions of approval were both
rare and moderate. The argument of the
right hon. gentleman was, that it was
impossible to have at once established
compulsory rating, and that as far
as many country districts were concerned, it
was better to leave the schools in the hands
of managers than in those of a reluctant
School Board; as the parson and the squire
often conducted these institutions more libe-
rally than would recalcitrant farmers, who
had to pay rates. He denied that any
material portion of the amount raised by rates
was devoted to the teaohing of religion, and
quoted the authority of Mrs. Anderson and
Mr. Cobden against compelling parents to
send their children to a particular school, or
excluding the reading of the Bible from all
schools. After an allusion to the resolutions
of the Birmingham League, and the resolu-
tion of the Conference at Manchester, the
right hon. gentleman appealed to Mr. Dixon,
whom he described as, like himself, not un-
familiar with machinery, not to stop the
operation of that which had been created
under the Education Act, or to throw it into
confusion by endeavouring to force upon the
country a thing for which it was not preparc
and to
__which it would never submit.

Mr. Liddell, Mr. Baokhouse, and Mr. Cor-
ranee were unanimous against the resolution;
and Mr. Atiberon-Ilerbert's support of it, on
the ground that publio instruction ought to be
purely secular, and that no common money

ought to be applied to forward any religious
opinions, was met by Lord B. Montagu with
the assertion that the motion "bristled with
compulsion," and was one hardly to be
expected from "an advanced Liberal."

Mr. Leatbam declared that nothing short of
the repeal of the objectionable clauses of the
Act of 1870 could satisfy the Nonconformists,
whom he represented as having, in regard to
this question, been wounded in their tenderest
point by those whom they had elevated to
power. He made a special reference to a
speech delivered by Mr. Knatabbull-Huges-
sea during the recess, which ho described as
" gasconading about the Qhurch," and some
of the expressions in which, he suggested,
mighdtasoeerathnektnle atnodfofregsetetrtihne strong meetnro ties of
minds as
to in
party in higher obligations.
According to the account of Mr. W. H.
Smith, the system of education, as at present
established, is working quite satisfactorily ;
and Dr. L. Playfair maintained most emphati-
cally that it was impossible to maintain
compulsion as to education if religious in-
struction ,was excluded from the sohools. _ _

Mr. Fawcett candidly admitted that he had
made a mistake when he placed his name to a
document in which it was maintained that the
Bible ought not to be explained in schools;
but upon economical rather than religious
grounds--not as a matter of conscience, but
as a suggestion of communism—he objected to
the provisions of tho Act of 1870 as to the pay-
ment of school fees out of the rates.

Mr. Mitchell Henry spoke amid continual
interruptions, which rendered his remarks
almostinaudible; but Mr. Greene created a
good deal of amusement by his declaration
that the sooner the Liberal party was dissolved
the better, and. his allusions to the "humbug
of the House." The supporters of the motion
the Conservative member for Bury St.
Edmunds denounced as a parcel of secularists,
infidels, and atheists, and the denunciation
was received with hearty laughter from the
Liberal benches.
The House divided about midnight, and
Mr. Dixon's resolutions were rejected, by a
majority of 261-355 to 94. Another division
was challenged upon the amendment of Mr.
Forster, which was carried by a majority of
226-323 to 98.

Some other business was disposed of, and
the House adjourned.

•
HOU'SE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDNY.
Mr. Charley moved the second reading of
the Infant Life Pioteotion Bill, and explained
that it was intended to carry out the object
which its title imports by enacting the princi-
pal recommendations of the select committee of
last year. After a very interesting discussion
the bill was read a second time. Mr. Wheel-
house moved the second reading of a bill to
render compulsory either upon the Poor-law

in the event of Mr. Stansfeld's bill on
the same subject receiving the sanction of the
House. Mr. ltathbone then moved the second
reading of the Municipal Officers' Superannua-
tion Bill, which gave rise to a debate,' but on
a division the motion was carried by 99 to 27.

articles.title: SUNDAY LA.BOUR, IN THE POST OFFICE,
articles.text:
SUNDAY LA.BOUR, IN THE POST
OFFICE,

•
To the Editor of the 11.Eil.thrt.

Sin,—This committee will thank you
warmly if you can permit space for this com-
munication, and so give an opportunity for
communicating to very many parishes the
newly promulgated rules as to postal work o'n
the Leril's day. The committee on Sunday
Labour in the Post Office, consisting of Lord
Dalhousie, Sir G. Gray, and Mr. Monsen, the
Postmaster Goueral, have presented their peti-
tion to the House of Parliament, and reeom-
Mend the following alterations in existing
rules :-
1. The old, rule that 'receivers Of six-
sevenths of Sunday letters must agree to the
cessation of Sunday delivery in a rural dis-
trict is revoked, and two-thirds substituted.
2. Memorialists may ask for cessation of
delivery, or of collection, or of both.
3. If, by tho vote of reeeivers of two•thirds
of the Sunday letters, a delivery or collection
be stopped, it can be resumed only by the vote
of the same proportion of receivers. This is
,most convenient, inasmuch as till now, while
it took six-sevenths to stop a post, there was
needed the vote of but one-seventh to ro-im-
'pose it.'
_ . . _ _

4. A Sunday delivery of letters in places
Where no such delivery has been usual can be
prevented by the vote of receivers of one-third
of the Sunday letters.
5. Where collections are made, both from
pillars and receiving houses, efforts are made
to limit the collection to one or the other.

6. To stop a Sunday delivery or collection
in a town there will still be demanded proof
of substantial unanimity amongst the inhabi7
tants in wishing for the abolition.
7. It is recommended that no letter carrier
who walks as Much as 14 miles on the week
days shall do any Sunday work, and the case
is to be met by the postal authorities paying a
substitute where a delivery or collection is in
upon, and in no case is a carrier to work
for two consecutive .Sundays.
8, The rule which permits any person to
refuse to receive letters on the Lord's day is
still in force, and should be widely used, for
under it each individual can show his ieg,ard
for the Divine Law, even though the commu-
nity among which he lives should persist in
enforcing Sunday, labour on the postal ser-
vants.

The new rule vill be a very decided gain.
Under the stringent six-sevenths rule 3,000
rural letter carriers have won the day of rest,
and it will be easy far many of the remaining
number to obtain their rest also under the
more liberal two-thirds rule.
The committee trust that under those fresh
regulations for which they earnestly struggled
with many, under the leadership of Mr. C,
Reed, the member for Hats Juicy, will en-
courage the clergy and god lypersons in very
many rural districts to secure rest for their
letter carriers. All needed information and.
suitable forms can be obtained from
JOHN GIUTTON.
Lord's Day Observance Society, 20, Jahn
Street, Adelphi, W.C.
March 1, 1872.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sta,,A.s you arc always ready tO take up
the cause of ,the working man, and are ever
ready to defend him against anything that is
:preposterous or absurd, I beg to hand yen a
sermon that was delivered a few weeks ago
frinn the pulpit of the parish church of Datlas-,
ton (Staffordshire), by the rooter of that
place. Not being much of a critic myself, and
having an opportunity of obtaining a copy of
i this precious doctrine n print, 1 beg to for-
ward one to you, with a hope that you will
i give a little comment upon it n your next im-
pression for your readers to form their own
opinion of what they might expect of some of
those reverend gentlemen, who tell us from
the pulpit ,to be docile, :servile, and obedient
servants; in all things obey your masters,.
emne what may, serve him with all your..
heart. If he attempts to reduce your wages,.
or require you to work more hours—if he in-
fringe WI your meal hours, or subject you to
the grossest tyranny, either from himself or
bullying foreman, submit to it without a:
murmur. Can anything be more ridiculous
.than, well teaching as this ? The Apostle
'Paul never intended a servant to obey an
earthly MastQr in all things; only our heavenly
Master. lie never intended any man or
woman because (hey were servants to be serfs.'
I listened to this sermon myself, and I confess

About twenty Minutes was appropriated to
telling the servants their duty towards their

masters, and abont two minutes in telling the

In my humble opinion a master's obligations
are as numerous towards a servant as are a
servant's towards a master. I can't see why
it does not take as many words to describe it
in the one case as it does in the other, if it is
done in an impartial manner. I need scarcely
state that this precious dogma has caused such
a bitter spirit of feeling amongst the working
portion of this town, that it will take this
reverend gentleman years to counteracf, if

will observe, that many servants were very

ness and evil that existed was caused by their
being paid very much more than they de-
served.

Now, sir, I should like to know if this same
thing is the cause oft he debanchery*e frequently
hear of existing amongst the class to which
the utterer of these words belongs. In my
simple opinion, the cause of these evils is the
result of the dissipated reckless excess of those
who indulge in them; which, I confess is one
of the greatest evils wo have to*contend with.
But one of these rev. zealots (I sea •by the
Daily Post, on the occasion of a stake of
agricultural labourers last week), advised themn
not to lay up treasure upon earth, but to be
'contented with their lot. He said he considered
that 12s. per week was enough for any man
with a family. Now, I sincerely believe th tt
if those low-paid disciples were placed on this
stipend for a few years it would be a sure cure
for the drunkenness that exists among their
class as well as others, which no one Would
•be more pleased to see than I. hit go on,
you agricultural labourers of WarWiekshire ;
you have set a noble example for your
brothers in other parts of the Country. Don't
listen to such advice as this parsoa gave you;
reject it as utterly useless ; you have trusted
to this ()lass too long,; they don't practise what
they, preadh. There are I admit honourable
exceptions ; some of them are sterling friends
to us as working men, but when we hoar some

leek-outs, and telling us from the 'pulpit that
We are being paid too MILO, and that they
consider that 12s. per week is enough for any
man with a family, it is enough to make us
break faith with them, and say "we believe you
are wolves in sheep's clothing." Cheer up,
agricultural labourers ; there is a brighter
future for you if you will only put your
shoulder to the wheel. These would-be arbi-
trary parsons will soon finish their eareer over
you, which no ono will rejoice at more, Mr.
i?,ditor, than yours faithfully,

articles.text:
LABOUR AND C,APITAL.--,_ THE MEA-
SURE OF EQUITY AND TRE LABOUR

NOTE.
To the Editor of the BEE-MvE•

Sir,--If one person exchanges his labour
against another, the first measure that suggests
itself forthe relative amount of labour performed
by each, is the length of time that each is ern-
nloyed. .11 all pursuits were equally laborious;
in other words, if all pursuits were equally
repugnant or toilsome, if it cost equal amounts
of human suffering or endurance, for each
hour of time employed in every different
pursuit, thou it would be exact equity to ex-
change one hour of labour for one other hour
of labour, r a product which has in it one hour
of labour for another product which has in it
one hour of labour, the world over. Such, how-
ever is not the case, and, though direct
comparisons between different kinds of labour
may be made, in order to arrive at a satis-
factory measure or equity, and the adoption
of a scientific system of cotillion°, it is
necessary : I.—That some method be devised
fur comparing the relative repugnance of
different kinds of labour. 2.—That in making
the comparison each individual should make

his or her own estimate of the repugnance to
him of the labour whith he performs, and 3.-
I:hat there should boa sufficient motive in the
results or consequenees to insure an 'wiliest
exercise of the judgment, and an honest ex-
pression of the real feelings of each in making
the comparison.•
1. That some method should be devised for
comparing the relative repugnance Of different
kinds of labour. All that is necessary is to
agree upon some particular kind of labour, the
averago repugnance of which is most easily.
ascertained, or the most nearly fixed, in the
locality or country, and use it as a standard of
comparison, a sort of yard-stick for measuring
the relative repugnance of other kinds of
labour. For example, in the Western States
of Ameriea, it is found that the most ap-
propriate kind of labour to be assumed as a
standard with which to compare all other
kinds of labour is corn raising. It is also
'found, upon extensive investigation, that the
average product of that kind of labour, in that
region; is twenty pounds of corn to the hour.
If, then, blacksmithing is reckoned as one half
harder work than corn-raising, it will be rated
(by the blacksmith himself) at thirty pounds
of corn to the hour., If. shoe-makihg is one
quarter less onerous than corn-raising, it will
ho rated as fifteen pounds of torn to the hour.
In this manner the idea of corn-raising is
used to measure the relative repugnance of all
kinds of labour.

2. In making the comparison, each in-
dividual must make his or her own estimate
of the repugnance to hien or her of the
particular labour which he or she performs.
This condition must be secured, for, basides,
there being differences in the hardness, or
repugnance of work, which all aro agreed
upon; there arc individual differences in the
feeling towards different kinds of labour,
whi,3ll makes the repugnance or attraction. of
one person for a particular kind of work quite
different from that of another, and because
another important principle in society is the
sovereignty of the individual. The individual
must be kept absolutely above all institutions.
lie must be free to abandon the principles
whenever he chooses. The only constraint
must be in the attractive nature and result of
true principles.

3. That there should be sufficient motive
in the results or consequences of, compliance
with these principles to. ensure an honest
OlCereiso of the judgment, an 4 an honest ex-
pression of the real feeling of each in making
his estimate of the relative repugnance of his
labour. The.existence of such a motive can
only be shown by a view of the general results
of the cost principle upon the, condition, of
society, and. upon the particular interests of
the individual. The force of a public senti•
Mont, rectified by the knowledge of true
rPrin-
ciples, will not be Jost sight of by a
.philo-
sophic mind; and the particular remedial
results of deviation from the principle of
equity upon the interests of the individual as
it affects his dealings with his felloWs will
be seen by the operations of the "labour note"
system. t-

If an exchange could always be m 143 and
completed on the spot, each party giving and
receiving an equivalent; that is, an amount
of labour or a product of labour just equal
to that in the labour or product for which it
was given or -received, the whole problem of
exchanges viduld be solved by this simple
method. There would be •in that 'ease, no
necessity for a circulating medium, or for any-
thing to perform that part which is performed
bymoney in our existing oommeroe. But such
is not the case. Articles are not always
at hand which have in them the same amount
.df cost;. indeed, it is the rare exception that
exact equivalents can be made upon the spot
in commodities which are mutually wanted.
Besides, it may frequently happen that one
wants something from another; either labour
or the products of labour, when that other, at
the time, wants nothing from him: In such a
case the exchange is only partially completed
on the spot, the remaining .part waiting to be
completed at some future time, by the perform-
ance of an equivalent amount of labour, ,or the
delivery of products having -in then' that
equivalent. - •

In such a case it is proper that the party
who does not make his part of the exehane
on the spot, should give an evidence of his
obligatien to do so at some future time ; and
this is the origin of the labour note, whieh is
the 'form assumed by equitable money. The
party who remains indebted to the other,
gives his note, provided the other consents to
receive it, for m equivalent amount of labour,
or else, as may be found convenient, of the
standard commodity—say so many pounds of
corn—specifying in the note the kind of labour
aiid. the alternative. The party reeAvine' the
note may not want the labour himself': btit
some person with Whom he deals may want it,
he-can then pass the note to the thud party
who is willing to receive it for an equivalent
amount of labour or product received from
him. In this manner the labour note bQgins
to circulate from one to another, and the aggre-
gate of labour notes in circulation in a neigh-
bourhood constitutes the neighbou,lood eir •
adding medium, 'dispensing so far as quit-
able coramercc extends, with money altogether

or, rather, introducing a new species of paper
money, representing what ought to be repre-
sented by a circulating medium, the exact
equivalent of the labour or commodity
rendered,- and issued solely upon individual
responsibility.
Under the labour note system, every man
who has in his ability to work, or in his chi-
meter, the assurance of responsibility, or the
basis of credit, has always by him as Much -
money as he needs. He has only to take his
pen from his pocket and make it at will.
Bankers are -proverbial for their anxiety to
maintain their credit unimpaired and unsua-
